sections.name: Ch 1 · Your Future in Health Care

items.q: What should students practice to prepare for health care programs and fields?
items.ex: Under the core quality 'work well with others,' the text tells students to practice good communication skills, which they can start now in school.
w: Help others have a better life.
This is a reason to enter health care, not a skill to practice.
Practice keeping secrets for privacy laws.
Respecting privacy is part of integrity, but the text doesn't tell students to practice keeping secrets for privacy laws.
The text recommends volunteering 'if you have the time,' not as often as possible.

alt.q: Which habit can a student build now that carries directly into health care work?
alt.ex: The text lists 'practice good communication skills' under the core quality of working well with others.
w: Holding back ideas is not good communication.
Cramming is discouraged in the text.
Health care requires working with others.

alt.q: A student wants to start acting like a health care professional while still in school. Which practice fits best?
alt.ex: Practicing communication in school prepares students for patient and team interactions.
w: Qualities can be practiced now in school.
Working with others is a core quality.

items.q: Which of the following is an example of objective data?
items.a: The score a student earns on a test
items.ex: A test score is measured, so it is objective data; opinions and feelings are subjective.
w: The students' opinions about a test's fairness
The nervousness the student experiences during a test
Nervousness is a feeling the student reports, so it is subjective.
The instructor's opinion about a test's difficulty
An opinion is subjective, even an instructor's.

alt.q: Which of these is subjective rather than objective data?
alt.a: A patient's report of feeling dizzy
alt.ex: Dizziness is reported by the patient and can't be measured directly.
w: A pulse counted at 88 beats a minute
A counted pulse is measured, so objective.
A weight of 150 pounds on a scale
A rash the nurse can see on the arm

alt.q: A medical assistant records four items. Which one is objective data?
alt.ex: A blood pressure reading is measured, so it is objective.
w: Patient says the pain is bad

items.q: Which health care career draws blood from patients for medical testing and from blood donors?
items.ex: Phlebotomists draw blood from patients for testing and from donors.
w: Nursing assistants help care for patients' basic needs, such as hygiene and feeding.
Laboratory technicians perform tests on specimens, such as preparing slides and counting cells.
Physician assistants can perform functions similar to those of physicians.

alt.q: A worker at a blood bank whose main task is collecting blood from donors is most likely a:
alt.ex: Collecting blood from donors is phlebotomy work.
w: Pharmacy techs help fill drug orders.

alt.q: What is the main job of a phlebotomist?
alt.a: Drawing blood for tests and donation
alt.ex: Phlebotomists collect blood for lab testing and for blood donation.
w: That is a medical records specialist.
Taking X-ray images of the chest

items.q: Which of the following challenges is most likely to be faced by an adult returning to school?
items.ex: The text names finding time to meet all their responsibilities as the most pressing problem for returning adults.
w: Memorizing isn't the main challenge named; learning means understanding.
Remembering the basics they learned in the past
The text doesn't name this as the main challenge.
Not the challenge the text emphasizes.

alt.q: An adult with a full-time job and two children goes back to school. What will most likely be the hardest part?
alt.ex: Juggling work, family, and classes makes time the biggest challenge.
w: The text names finding time, not reading, as the most pressing problem.
Not the challenge the text names.
Not the challenge named; time is.

alt.q: According to the text, many returning adult students struggle most with:
alt.a: Time to meet all their duties
alt.ex: Adults often juggle classes, studying, family, and jobs.
w: A lack of any prior work experience
Too much free time each week
The problem is too little time.
Not the problem the text names.

items.q: Which health care career performs a variety of tasks related to the collection, organization, and maintenance of patient data?
items.ex: Medical records specialists organize records, code, enter data, and compile reports.
w: Transcriptionists prepare written medical reports, often from voice recordings.
Nurse aides give basic patient care.

alt.q: Assigning codes to diagnoses and keeping patient files organized is the work of a:
alt.ex: Coding and organizing records are medical records specialist tasks.

alt.q: Which occupation is in the health information management category?
alt.ex: Medical records specialists manage patient data, so they are in HIM.
w: Nursing assisting is therapeutic and treatment.

items.q: What level of education is required for a Biomedical Equipment Technician?
items.ex: Table 1–20 lists an associate's degree for the biomedical equipment technician; biomedical engineers need a bachelor's degree or higher.
w: Table 1–20 lists an associate's degree for this technician.
Table 1–20 lists a bachelor's or higher for biomedical engineers, not technicians.
A doctorate is far beyond the requirement.

alt.q: A student wants to repair and maintain hospital equipment as a biomedical equipment technician. What education should they usually plan on?
alt.ex: Table 1–20 lists an associate's degree for biomedical equipment technicians.
w: That is more than usually required.

alt.q: Which statement about biomedical equipment technician training is accurate?
alt.ex: Table 1–20 lists an associate's degree for biomedical equipment technicians.
w: A doctoral degree is usually expected

items.q: Which of the following health care professions are trained to perform a variety of duties in the dental office?
items.ex: Dental assistants handle many duties in the dental office, such as passing instruments and suctioning the mouth.
w: Physical therapists help patients regain movement.
Medical assistants work in medical, not dental, offices.
Registered nurses work in settings such as hospitals, clinics, and long-term care.

alt.q: Who in a dental office passes instruments to the dentist and suctions the patient's mouth?
alt.ex: Passing instruments and suctioning are dental assistant duties.
w: Hygienists clean teeth and give preventive care.
Lab techs make crowns and dentures.
Medical assistants work in medical offices.

alt.q: A person who wants a varied job helping dentists chairside and in the office should look into becoming a:
alt.ex: Dental assistants perform a variety of chairside and office duties.
w: They work in a lab making dental appliances.

items.q: What education must a registered radiologic assistant obtain?
items.ex: Table 1–16 lists a bachelor's degree for the registered radiologic assistant, with voluntary registration from the ARRT.
w: Table 1–16 lists an associate's or bachelor's for radiographers; this role lists a bachelor's.
Table 1–16 lists a bachelor's degree for this role.

alt.q: A radiographer may enter with an associate's degree. What education does the text list for a registered radiologic assistant?
alt.ex: Table 1–16 lists a bachelor's degree for the registered radiologic assistant; radiographers need an associate's or bachelor's degree.
w: That is the radiographer's entry level; this role needs a bachelor's.
That is the path for radiologists, who are physicians.

alt.q: What degree does the text list for a registered radiologic assistant?
alt.ex: Table 1–16 lists a bachelor's degree for the registered radiologic assistant.
w: Radiographers need an associate's or bachelor's; this role lists a bachelor's.

items.q: Which of the following type of data best describes what others say or want and cannot be directly measured?
items.ex: Subjective data are what people report, such as feelings, opinions, and symptoms, which cannot be directly measured.
w: Objective data can be observed or measured.
Not a term used in the text.
Not a term used in the text.

alt.q: A patient says, 'My stomach feels upset.' What kind of data is this?
alt.ex: The patient is reporting a feeling that can't be measured.
w: Objective data are measured or observed.
Findings that can be observed are objective.

alt.q: Which description fits subjective data?
alt.a: What a person reports, not measurable
alt.ex: Subjective data come from what the person says and can't be measured.
w: What a provider can see, hear, or measure
Lab results printed on a chart report
Numbers read from a medical device

items.q: Which of the following is a noted important core quality for health care professionals?
items.a: Have compassion and integrity for patients, co-workers, and the workplace.
items.ex: Caring about others (compassion) and having integrity are among the essential core qualities the text lists.
w: Work at a fast pace and focus on only one task at a time.
Not a listed core quality; the text stresses being flexible and adapting to change.
Complete externship with a positive outlook.
Finishing an externship is a program step, not a core quality.
Help others have a better life.
This is a reward of the work, not a personal quality.

alt.q: Which pair of traits appears among the core qualities of health care professionals?
alt.ex: Caring about others and integrity are both core qualities.
w: Not on the core list; teamwork is.
Flexibility, not rigidity, is a core quality.

alt.q: Which is NOT one of the core qualities the text describes?
alt.ex: Working well with others is a core quality, so avoiding teamwork is not.

items.q: A career in health care can be very satisfying because
items.a: you can help others have a better life.
items.ex: The text says health care work makes a difference in the quality of life of those served, though it also makes many demands.
w: most health care jobs are not very demanding.
The text says health care work is demanding.
the pay is higher than for most jobs in other industries.
The text doesn't claim higher pay than other industries.
Many jobs require formal education and credentials.

alt.q: What does the text give as a key reason health care work can be rewarding?
alt.a: It lets you improve others' lives
alt.ex: Helping others is what makes the demanding work satisfying.
w: It has short and easy work hours
Health care can involve long hours.
It pays more than all other fields
It needs little training to enter

alt.q: Which statement about health care careers is accurate?
alt.ex: The text calls health care work satisfying but demanding.
w: They are easy and low in stress
They always pay the highest wages

items.q: What is the first step in a good problem-solving process?
items.ex: Problem-solving starts by clearly identifying the real problem, since what first appears to be the problem may be only a symptom.
w: Think about whether the problem can be solved.
Not a step in the five-step process.
Brainstorming solutions (creating alternatives) is step three.

alt.q: In the five-step problem-solving process, which step comes before gathering information?
alt.ex: Identifying the problem is step one; gathering information is step two.

alt.q: Jordan's poor job evaluation turned out to be a symptom of unreliable transportation. Which problem-solving step does this discovery belong to?
alt.ex: Finding the real problem behind a symptom is step one.
w: Gathering facts comes after naming the problem.

items.q: Which of the following occupations is expected to have the highest increase in positions between 2021 and 2031?
items.a: Home health and personal care aides
items.ex: Home health and personal care aides are projected to add about 924,000 positions, the largest numerical increase.
w: Medical assistants add about 117,800 (Table 1–2), far fewer.
Physicians are not among Table 1–2's largest increases.
Physical therapists grow 17% (Table 1–1) but aren't in Table 1–2.

alt.q: Which occupation is projected to add about 924,000 positions from 2021 to 2031?
alt.a: Home health and personal care aides
alt.ex: This is the largest numerical increase in Table 1–2.
w: Medical assistants add about 117,800; phlebotomists aren't in Table 1–2.
Neither is in Table 1–2's largest numerical increases.

alt.q: Registered nurses are projected to add about 195,400 jobs from 2021 to 2031. Which occupation will add more?
alt.a: Home health and personal care aides
alt.ex: Aides are projected to add about 924,000 jobs.
w: They grow 24% (Table 1–1) but aren't in Table 1–2.

items.q: What are the two common accrediting agencies for health care programs?
items.a: Commission on Accreditation of Allied Health Programs (CAAHEP) and Accrediting Bureau of Health Education Schools (ABHES)
items.ex: CAAHEP and ABHES are the two common accrediting agencies for health care programs; NCLEX and MCAT are exams.
w: Commission on Accreditation of Allied Health Programs (CAAHEP) and National Council Licensing Examination (NCLEX)
NCLEX is a nursing licensing exam, not an accreditor.
Accrediting Bureau of Health Education Schools (ABHES) and Medical Assisting Education Review Board (MAERB)
MAERB is not one of the two agencies the text names.
National Council Licensing Examination (NCLEX) and Medical College Admission Test (MCAT)
Both are exams, not accrediting agencies.

alt.q: A student wants to confirm that a health care program meets recognized standards. Which pair of agencies might have accredited it?
alt.ex: These two are the common accrediting agencies named in the text.
w: These are government agencies, not accreditors.

alt.q: What do CAAHEP and ABHES have in common?
alt.ex: Both are accrediting agencies for health care schools and programs.
w: AAMA and AMT grant MA credentials.

items.q: Which of the following physical therapy occupations does not require testing and licensure?
items.ex: Table 1–11 lists 'None' for testing and licensure of physical therapist aides, who train on the job or in a vocational program; PTAs and PTs are regulated.
w: Not an actual occupation title in the text.
Physical therapists must pass an exam and be licensed.
PTAs need licensure, certification, or registration in all states.

alt.q: Which physical therapy worker could start the job without passing a licensing exam?
alt.ex: PT aides have no testing or licensure requirement.
w: PTAs must be licensed, certified, or registered.

alt.q: Which statement about physical therapy occupations is accurate?
alt.a: Aides need no license to work
alt.ex: Aides train on the job or in a vocational program, while PTAs and PTs are regulated.
w: PTAs are regulated in all states.
Therapists need no exam to work
Aides must pass a national exam
Table 1–11 lists no testing for aides.

items.q: Which medical specialist promotes wellness and treats children?
items.ex: Pediatricians promote wellness and treat illness in children.
w: Obstetricians care for women during pregnancy and childbirth.
Emergency providers treat acute illnesses and injuries.

alt.q: A parent needs a provider for a toddler's checkups and illnesses. Which specialist fits best?
alt.ex: Pediatricians care for children.

alt.q: A gerontologist works with older persons. Which provider works with the opposite end of the age range?
alt.ex: Pediatricians work with children.

items.q: Jaime is trying to decide whether to study to become a surgical technologist or an emergency medical technician. Which of the following criteria would be best for making a decision that will most likely result in them being satisfied with their career?
items.a: Their preferences for workplace environment and conditions
items.ex: The text's EMT example shows that work conditions (long shifts, nights, all weather) must be weighed to choose a career with long-term satisfaction; workplace preferences are a listed personal factor.
w: The length of time necessary to complete the required education
The text lists time for education as a factor, but it doesn't predict satisfaction with the work.
The career choices of their friends
Friends' choices don't reflect Jaime's own preferences.
Which programs are offered at local schools
Convenience doesn't predict satisfaction with the work.

alt.q: Jaime is choosing between surgical technologist and EMT. What would most help them predict which job's daily work they would enjoy?
alt.ex: Matching the setting to their preferences predicts satisfaction.
w: Speed of training doesn't predict satisfaction.
Friends' choices don't reflect Jaime's preferences.
Which school is nearest to home

alt.q: Surgical technologists work in sterile operating rooms, while EMTs work long shifts outdoors in all weather. Why should Jaime consider these differences?
alt.ex: Preferred environment and conditions are a key personal factor in choosing a career.
w: They determine the cost of tuition
They decide which school will accept them
They show which job pays the most
The text doesn't base choice on pay.

items.q: Which of the following is an example of moving up the career ladder?
items.a: A physical therapist assistant who returns to school to become a physical therapist
items.ex: Moving up the career ladder means getting more education to reach a higher level, such as going from PTA to physical therapist.
w: A dental hygienist who earns a raise in salary
A raise keeps the same position level.
A registered nurse who is promoted to a supervisory position
A promotion within the same occupation doesn't move to a higher education level.
A medical assistant who receives increased responsibilities
More duties in the same job don't change the career ladder level.

alt.q: Which move goes UP a career ladder from one level to the next?
alt.a: A nursing assistant becoming an LPN
alt.ex: LPN is a higher level that requires more education than CNA.
w: An RN moving to a different hospital
An LPN switching to night shifts
A pharmacist becoming a pharmacy tech

alt.q: A pharmacy technician wants to climb the career ladder. Which plan fits?
alt.a: Go to school to become a pharmacist
alt.ex: Pharmacist is the professional level above technician.
w: Ask for a raise as a pharmacy tech
A raise keeps the same level.
Move to a new pharmacy as a tech
Train new techs at the same pharmacy
Extra duties at the same level.

items.q: Which of the following will not help students prepare themselves for health care educational programs and future jobs?
items.a: Learning only what is needed to pass tests
items.ex: Learning only enough to pass tests leaves students unprepared; they need to understand and apply what they learn.
w: Reading for comprehension is a recommended study skill.
Volunteering builds skills and career knowledge.
Asking themselves questions about what they are learning or doing
Asking questions helps students learn and think.

alt.q: Which habit best prepares a student for a future health care job?
alt.ex: Learning means understanding information so it can be applied to new situations.
w: Learning only what will be on the exam
Students need more than test content.
Skipping volunteer work to study more

alt.q: A student says, 'I just need to learn what's on the test.' Why is this a poor approach for a health care student?
alt.a: Patients rely on what workers truly know
alt.ex: Mistakes on the job can have serious consequences, and students who study only to pass tests may lack the long-term knowledge needed.
w: Tests cover everything they will need
Tests can't cover everything for a career.
Memorizing is the best way to learn facts

items.q: A patient has pain during a therapy session at the clinic with the physical therapist assistant. To whom should the physical therapist assistant report the patient's pain?
items.ex: Physical therapist assistants work under the supervision of a physical therapist to carry out treatment plans and document progress, so changes such as pain go to the PT.
w: Aides support therapists and assistants; they don't direct care.
The manager handles operations, not the patient's treatment plan.
Not a title in Table 1–11; PTAs work under the physical therapist.

alt.q: A PTA works under whose supervision?
alt.ex: PTAs carry out treatment plans under a physical therapist.
w: Aides have less training than PTAs.

alt.q: During exercises, a patient tells the PTA their knee hurts more than usual. What should the PTA do?
alt.a: Report it to the physical therapist
alt.ex: The supervising PT needs to know about new or increased pain.
w: Ignore it and finish the exercises
Tell the aide to adjust the plan
Wait to mention it at the next visit

items.q: Which of the following terms is used to describe an understanding of exactly what one is legally allowed to do in one’s profession?
items.ex: Scope of practice means understanding exactly what one is legally allowed to do in one's profession.
w: Licensure is government permission to practice, not the limits of tasks.
Bias is a belief, usually negative, about a group.
Certification means meeting set standards, usually by exam.

alt.q: A medical assistant is asked to do a task they aren't legally allowed to do. Which concept tells them to decline?
alt.ex: Scope of practice sets the tasks a worker may legally perform.
w: Bias is a belief about a group.

alt.q: Which statement describes scope of practice?
alt.a: The tasks a worker may legally perform
alt.ex: Scope of practice is about legal limits on job tasks.
w: The list of workers who passed an exam
The total hours a worker may be on duty
A worker's negative beliefs about a group

items.q: It is expected that between 2021 and 2031, the number of jobs that will be created in the health care industry is
items.ex: The BLS projects about 2 million new health care jobs (13% growth) from 2021 to 2031.
w: Too low; about 2 million are projected.
Too high; the projection is about 2 million.
Too high; the projection is about 2 million.

alt.q: The BLS projects health care employment will grow 13% from 2021 to 2031. About how many new jobs is that?
alt.ex: 13% growth equals about 2 million new jobs.
w: 22 million is the total current jobs.

alt.q: Which projection for 2021–2031 health care jobs is accurate?
alt.ex: The BLS projects 13% growth and about 2 million new jobs, faster than the average for all occupations.
w: 25% is the home health aide rate.

items.q: What is the purpose of standards for health care professionals?
items.a: Protecting the public from harm caused by incompetence
items.ex: Standards protect the public by ensuring professionals have at least the minimum knowledge and skills to practice safely.
w: Determining the amount of education necessary for various occupations
Education levels vary, but that isn't the purpose of standards.
Maintaining lists of health care professionals for referrals
Tracking the quality of health care training programs
Program quality is the job of accreditation.

alt.q: Why do licensure and certification standards exist for health care workers?
alt.a: To keep the public safe from incompetence
alt.ex: Standards ensure minimum competence to protect the public.
w: To limit the number of people in each field
To raise the pay of credentialed workers
To rank schools by the quality of programs

alt.q: A state requires a license to practice and continuing education to keep it. Whom does this mainly protect?
alt.ex: Ongoing standards protect the public from harm caused by incompetence.
w: The board enforces rules; it isn't the one protected.

items.q: A nurse works on the medical floor of a large hospital. One of the patients was recently diagnosed with diabetes (a condition in which the body does not produce enough insulin to control blood sugar levels). Early one morning when reviewing the patient's chart, the nurse notices that the physician was in the previous evening and ordered the patient's blood sugar to be checked at 8:00 am. The results will determine if insulin is to be given. (The higher the blood sugar level is, the greater the amount of insulin to be given.) When the nurse goes to check the patient's blood sugar level at 7:45 am, they discover that the patient has just finished eating breakfast. The nurse considers what they know about diabetes: after eating, an individual's blood sugar normally increases for a few hours. What should the nurse do about the patient's blood test?
items.a: Contact the patient's physician and inform them about the breakfast schedule
items.ex: Testing right after breakfast would give a falsely high blood sugar and too much insulin, so the nurse should contact the physician about the timing.
w: Wait until tomorrow and perform the blood test before breakfast
Delaying a day ignores the order without the physician's input.
Perform the test as directed in the order
Testing after eating gives a falsely high result and too much insulin.
Ignore the order and take the blood test later
Changing the order on their own is outside the nurse's role.

alt.q: A patient's blood sugar test, which sets the insulin dose, is due right after they finish breakfast. Why is this a problem?
alt.a: The result will be falsely high
alt.ex: Blood sugar rises for a few hours after eating.
w: The result will be falsely low
Insulin cannot be given after meals
Not the issue; the dose would be too high.
The test can't be done before 8:00

alt.q: A nurse notices an ordered blood sugar test would fall right after the patient's breakfast and calls the physician. What does this show about thinking like a health care professional?
alt.a: Question orders that don't fit the facts
alt.ex: Professionals apply knowledge and raise concerns with the provider.
w: Always follow every order exactly as written
Change the order yourself when you are unsure
Skip any test that seems to be unnecessary

items.q: If a student wants to combine mechanical skills and working with patients, which of the following careers is most likely a good fit?
items.ex: Sonographers operate ultrasound equipment and need technical aptitude plus the ability to communicate with patients, combining both interests.
w: BMETs install, test, service, and repair equipment; the text describes no patient care.
The text describes lab technicians running tests on specimens, not working with patients.
Pharmacy technicians fill drug orders and manage drug inventory.

alt.q: Which job combines operating technical equipment with hands-on patient contact?
alt.ex: Sonographers run ultrasound equipment on patients.
w: Mechanical work but little patient contact.

alt.q: A student loves fixing machines but would miss working with patients. Why might biomedical equipment technician be a poor fit?
alt.ex: The text describes BMETs as installing, testing, servicing, and repairing equipment, not caring for patients.
w: It is mostly patient bathing work
It is illegal without a medical degree

items.q: Your school has a strict attendance policy, and you know that if you miss one more day, you will fail your current classes. On Saturday, your car breaks down, and you do not know how you will get to class on Monday. What should you do?
items.a: Gather information about your options and choose the option of carpooling with a friend
items.ex: Gathering information and choosing a workable alternative follows the problem-solving process.
w: Drop your classes, as attending school is just too stressful
Dropping classes avoids the problem instead of solving it.
Try calling your instructors to let them know you have an emergency
Calling doesn't solve the transportation problem.
Worry all weekend and complain to friends about your problem
Worrying and complaining take no action.

alt.q: Your car broke down, and missing class Monday means failing. After identifying the real problem as getting to class, what should you do next?
alt.a: Look into ride options you have
alt.ex: Gathering information is the step after identifying the problem.
w: Email instructors to ask for a pass
That doesn't solve getting to class.
Plan to drop the classes Monday
Wait to see if the car fixes itself

alt.q: Your car breaks down, and missing one more class means failing. Which response shows good problem-solving?
alt.ex: It gathers information, then chooses and acts on an alternative.
w: Missing class and hoping for mercy
Dropping out to avoid the stress

items.q: The career with the largest projected percentage increase in employment between 2021 and 2031 is
items.ex: Nurse practitioners have the largest projected percentage increase, 46%.
w: PT aides are part of a 24% group.
Dental assistants are projected to grow 8%.
Physician assistants grow 28%, second to NPs.

alt.q: Which occupation is projected to grow 46% between 2021 and 2031?
alt.ex: NPs have the highest percentage growth in Table 1–1.

alt.q: Physician assistants are projected to grow 28%. Which occupation grows by a larger percentage?
alt.ex: NPs are projected to grow 46%.

items.q: The career expected to have the largest numerical increase in employment between 2021 and 2031 is
items.ex: Home health and personal care aides are projected to add about 924,000 jobs, the largest numerical increase.
w: Medical secretaries aren't in Table 1–2's largest increases.
Physicians aren't in Table 1–2's largest increases.

alt.q: Which occupation is projected to add the most actual jobs, even though it isn't the highest growth rate?
alt.ex: Aides add about 924,000 jobs, the most in number.

alt.q: About how many positions are home health and personal care aides projected to add from 2021 to 2031?
alt.ex: This is the largest numerical increase in Table 1–2.
w: That is the whole industry's new jobs.

items.q: Which of the following factors is most important for students to consider as they make a career choice?
items.a: Their aptitude for the tasks they would be performing in the chosen career
items.ex: The text says career choices should match students' preferences and abilities; natural abilities are among the personal factors to weigh.
w: The number of jobs available in their geographic area
Job availability matters but doesn't ensure fit.
The cost of the necessary education
Cost matters but doesn't predict success.
The amount of time necessary for education and training
The text lists time for education as a factor, but matching abilities to the work is key.

alt.q: A student is calm, good with their hands, and likes precise work. Why should these traits guide their career choice?
alt.a: Abilities that fit the job aid success
alt.ex: Natural abilities that match the work lead to success and satisfaction.
w: They decide which program costs the least
They guarantee a job in any field
They matter only for aide positions

alt.q: Which career-choice factor is about the person rather than the program?
alt.ex: Natural abilities are a personal factor the text says to consider.
w: Tuition and fees for the program
That is about the job market.

items.q: If a school is accredited, this means that it
items.a: Has met standards set by an accrediting Agency
items.ex: Accreditation means the school or program has met the standards of an accrediting agency.
w: Accreditation isn't about offering advanced degrees.
Accredited schools can offer many kinds of programs.
Can offer career services to its graduates
Career services aren't what accreditation means.

alt.q: How does a school usually earn accreditation?
alt.a: It applies and passes a site visit
alt.ex: A team from the agency visits to confirm standards are met.
w: It pays a fee to the state board
Its graduates all pass a licensing exam

alt.q: Why might a student choose an accredited program?
alt.ex: Most examining and licensing boards require attending an accredited school and/or program.
w: It guarantees a job after school

items.q: Which of the following careers would a student investigate further if they enjoy working with detailed paperwork?
items.ex: Health information management workers gather, organize, store, and document patient information, which involves detailed paperwork.
w: MRI technologists perform imaging with patients.
Ophthalmic lab technicians make eyeglass lenses.

alt.q: Which job category suits someone who likes organizing detailed records?
alt.ex: HIM occupations manage patient records and data.

alt.q: A health information technician spends most of the day:
alt.ex: HIM work centers on records and coding.
w: Drawing blood from patients and donors
Taking X-rays and MRI scans of patients

items.q: A student enjoys listening to their instructor's lectures and reading the textbook in their Introduction to Health Care course. They are not interested in doing group projects with their classmates as they prefer to work alone and not communicate with others. How is this likely to affect their future career success if they choose a career in health care?
items.a: Negatively because work in health care requires communicating well with others
items.ex: Working well with others, including good communication and being a good team member, is a core quality for health care professionals.
w: No effect because most health care professionals work on their own
Most health care professionals work in teams.
Positively because they will not waste time socializing with coworkers
Communicating with coworkers is part of the job, not wasted time.
No effect as long as they perform their work

sc.title: Emilio and Dr. Bennett
sc.text:
Emilio had always dreamed of becoming a veterinarian technician. After years of hard work and dedication, Emilio finally achieved this goal and began a career at a busy animal hospital. Emilio was excited to learn that the person they would be working directly under is Dr. Sarah Bennett, a seasoned veterinarian with a wealth of knowledge and experience.

During the first few weeks on the job, Emilio worked closely under Dr. Bennett, absorbing every piece of advice and instruction. Dr. Bennett made a point to provide instruction and constructive feedback at every opportunity, guiding Emilio through complex cases and offering insights into effective patient care.

After a few weeks in the new role, Emilio noticed a difference in how Dr. Bennett interacted with the other veterinarian technicians. While Dr. Bennett was patient and supportive with Emilio, they often seemed short-tempered and critical towards the other technicians, offering little guidance and frequently pointing out mistakes without offering solutions. Emilio even noticed one of the other technicians posting on their social media about recent interactions with Dr. Bennett, stating in the post, “this is the worst vet I have ever worked with, don’t take your pets there.”

items.q: How does Emilio's experience working under Dr. Bennett demonstrate the importance of professionalism in the veterinary field?
items.a: Emilio's interaction with Dr. Bennett underscores the importance of humility and willingness to learn in veterinary practice.
items.ex: Emilio's eagerness to absorb advice and feedback shows the humility and willingness to learn that professionalism requires.
w: Emilio's experience highlights the need for strict adherence to rules and regulations in veterinary clinics.
The scenario is about learning and feedback, not rules.
Emilio's role under Dr. Bennett illustrates the limited opportunities for growth and mentorship available to veterinarian technicians.
Emilio received strong mentorship, the opposite.
Emilio's observations emphasize the significance of competition and rivalry among veterinarian technicians in the workplace.
Nothing in the scenario shows rivalry.

alt.q: Which of Emilio's behaviors best shows professionalism?
alt.ex: Openness to instruction shows willingness to learn.
w: Competing hard with the other technicians
Emilio worked closely with Dr. Bennett.

alt.q: What attitude did Emilio show by taking in Dr. Bennett's instruction?
alt.ex: Absorbing advice reflects humility and openness to learning.

w: 75.6 years is not the text's figure.

alt.q: Life expectancy for people born in 1900 was 47 years. What is today's projected figure for males?
alt.ex: Males now have a projected life expectancy of 73.2 years.
w: That was for people born in 1900.

alt.q: Which pair correctly gives projected life expectancy for males and females?
alt.ex: The text gives 73.2 years for males and 79.1 for females.
w: Those are the 1900 and 1950 overall figures.

items.q: What percentage of certain costs are covered by Medicare?
items.ex: In some instances Medicare pays only 80% of certain costs, leaving 20% that many people can't afford.
w: 20% is the share left for the patient or supplemental insurance.
65 is the eligibility age, not a percentage.

alt.q: If Medicare pays its usual share of a $1,000 covered cost, how much might be left for the patient or a supplemental plan?
alt.ex: Medicare pays 80% ($800), leaving 20%, or $200.
w: Medicare doesn't always pay the full cost.

alt.q: Why do many older adults struggle with costs that Medicare covers at 80%?
alt.a: They can't afford coverage for the other 20%
alt.ex: Many can't afford supplemental insurance for the remaining 20%.
w: Medicare stops paying after one hospital visit
Medicaid refuses anyone who has Medicare
They must pay the full 80% share themselves

items.q: Disorders caused by mental or emotional factors are known as psychosomatic disorders.
items.ex: Psychosomatic disorders are caused by mental or emotional factors, and their physical symptoms are real.
items.ww: The text defines psychosomatic disorders exactly this way.

alt.q: A psychosomatic illness is imaginary and exists only in the patient's head.
alt.ex: Psychosomatic symptoms are real physical results of what's happening in the mind.
alt.ww: They are not 'all in one's head.'

alt.q: Physical symptoms that arise from emotional stress are an example of a psychosomatic disorder.
alt.ex: Psychosomatic disorders come from mental or emotional factors.
alt.ww: Mental and emotional factors can cause real physical symptoms.

items.q: What is the transplantation of normal genes into cells in place of missing or defective ones to correct genetic disorders?
items.ex: Gene therapy transplants normal genes into cells to replace missing or defective ones and correct genetic disorders.
w: Targeted drug therapy attacks specific cancer cells.
Genomics studies genes; it doesn't replace them.
An organ transplant replaces a whole organ, not genes.

alt.q: A researcher inserts working copies of a gene into a child's cells to fix an inherited disorder. What is this called?
alt.ex: Replacing faulty genes with normal ones is gene therapy.
w: That uses tiny doses of substances.

alt.q: What does gene therapy aim to correct?
alt.a: Genetic disorders caused by faulty genes
alt.ex: Gene therapy corrects genetic disorders by replacing missing or defective genes.
w: Cancer cells by attacking them with drugs
Organ failure by using a donor's organ
Energy blocks using thin needles in the skin

items.q: What year was the first "test tube" baby born in England?
items.ex: The first 'test tube' baby was born in England in 1978.
w: 1997 is when a sheep was cloned.

alt.q: Which milestone occurred in 1978?
alt.ex: England saw the birth of the first test tube baby in 1978.

alt.q: Which of these happened earliest?
alt.a: Test tube baby born in England
alt.ex: The test tube baby (1978) came before AIDS (1981), cloning (1997), and the 2015 initiative.

items.q: What year was the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act signed into law?
items.ex: The Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act was signed into law in 2010.

alt.q: The Affordable Care Act became law in which year?
alt.ex: It was signed into law in 2010.
w: That's when a sheep was cloned.

alt.q: Which event happened in 2010?
alt.a: The Affordable Care Act was signed
alt.ex: The ACA was signed into law in 2010.

items.q: What are ambulatory services also known as?
items.ex: Ambulatory services, for patients who don't require hospitalization, are also called outpatient services.
w: Nursing homes give long-term residential care.

alt.q: A patient has a procedure at a surgery center and goes home 2 hours later. What type of care is this?
alt.ex: Care without a hospital stay is ambulatory, or outpatient, care.
w: That's a hospital unit before discharge.

alt.q: Which statement about ambulatory services is accurate?
alt.a: They serve patients who don't need to be admitted
alt.ex: Ambulatory services are for patients who don't require hospitalization.
w: They provide 24-hour nursing for long-term residents
They transport patients by ambulance to hospitals
They account for very little patient care today
They account for most patient care.

items.q: What is the promotion of health through preventative measures and the practice of good health habits?
items.ex: Wellness is the promotion of health through preventive measures and the practice of good health habits.
w: Holistic medicine considers the whole person.
Life expectancy is how long people are expected to live.
Integrative medicine combines Western and complementary care.

alt.q: A center offers immunizations, exercise classes, and nutrition education to keep people healthy. Which concept does it promote?
alt.ex: Wellness centers promote health through prevention and good habits.
w: That relieves symptoms; it doesn't prevent disease.

alt.q: How does the concept of wellness differ from the traditional view of health?
alt.a: It goes beyond simply being free of disease
alt.ex: Wellness means more than the absence of disease.
w: It focuses only on curing diseases once found
It depends mainly on specialist treatment
Wellness relies on personal health habits.
It means having no chronic conditions at all
Wellness goes beyond absence of disease.

items.q: Around how many years ago was the importance of handwashing discovered?
items.ex: The importance of handwashing was discovered less than 200 years ago, when Ignaz Semmelweis linked physician hand contamination to deaths.
w: 100 years is too recent; it was earlier than that.
Over 500 years is far too long ago.

alt.q: About when was the importance of handwashing in preventing infection recognized?
alt.ex: Handwashing's importance was discovered less than 200 years ago.

alt.q: A coworker says handwashing has been standard medical practice for thousands of years. What is accurate?
alt.a: It was discovered under 200 years ago
alt.ex: Its importance was recognized less than 200 years ago.
w: They're right; it dates to ancient times
It was first recognized about 1,000 years ago
It was first recognized after the year 2000

sc.title: Roseanna - discharge planning and Medicare
sc.text:
Henry Dodson, a social worker for a hospital, is working on care coordination for Roseanna, a 93-year-old patient discharging to a nursing facility after a hip fracture from a fall at home. Henry notices that Roseanna has Medicare insurance coverage. Roseanna has no living

relatives and lives alone in a one-story house. Henry believes that Roseanna will require a long-term stay in the nursing facility and is unsure that Roseanna will ever return to living at the home alone.

items.q: Henry knows that the following is true of Medicare coverage with nursing facilities
items.a: Medicare does not provide coverage for assisted living or long-term stays in a nursing facility.
items.ex: Medicare covers only short-term nursing home stays after hospitalization and does not cover assisted living or long-term stays.
w: Medicare does not provide any coverage for short-term stays in a nursing facility.
Medicare does cover short-term stays after hospitalization.
Medicare covers short-term and long-term stays in a nursing facility following hospitalization.
Medicare does not cover long-term stays.
Medicare always covers nursing facility stays following hospitalization for hip fractures.
Coverage isn't automatic for any diagnosis; it's limited to short-term stays.

alt.q: Henry expects Roseanna to need a long-term stay. Which program could help pay for long-term nursing home care if Roseanna qualifies by income?
alt.ex: State Medicaid programs cover nursing home care for people with low incomes.
w: Covers only short stays after hospitalization.

alt.q: Which part of Roseanna's nursing facility stay could Medicare help pay for?
alt.a: A short stay right after the hospitalization
alt.ex: Medicare covers only short-term nursing home stays after a hospital stay.
w: The entire long-term stay, however long
Assisted living if Roseanna moves there
Any stay, as long as it follows a hip fracture
The diagnosis doesn't change the limit.

sc.title: Roseanna - discharge planning and Medicare
sc.text:
Henry Dodson, a social worker for a hospital, is working on care coordination for Roseanna, a 93-year-old patient discharging to a nursing facility after a hip fracture from a fall at home. Henry notices that Roseanna has Medicare insurance coverage. Roseanna has no living

relatives and lives alone in a one-story house. Henry believes that Roseanna will require a long-term stay in the nursing facility and is unsure that Roseanna will ever return to living at the home alone.

items.q: Roseanna will be prescribed pain medication at discharge. Roseanna's nurse explains the risk of overuse and explains that Roseanna will not become addicted if the pain medications are used as prescribed, including the correct dose and time. This is an example of what measure to prevent pain medication overuse?
items.a: Educating patients about the risks of pain medication
items.ex: Explaining the risk of overuse and how to take the medication safely is educating patients about the risks of pain medication.
w: This targets forged prescriptions, not patient teaching.
Teaching patients other methods for controlling pain
Teaching other methods would mean nondrug pain control.
Regulating pain clinics is a policy measure.

alt.q: Which nurse action would be an example of educating Roseanna about pain medication risks?
alt.a: Explaining what happens if doses are exceeded
alt.ex: Telling patients about overuse dangers is educating them about the risks.
w: Teaching Roseanna to use ice and relaxation for pain
Checking that the prescription isn't forged
Reviewing state rules for local pain clinics

alt.q: If Roseanna's nurse instead taught Roseanna breathing exercises and heat packs to manage pain, which measure would that be?
alt.a: Teaching other methods for controlling pain
alt.ex: Nondrug pain-control methods fall under teaching other ways to control pain.
w: Educating patients about pain medication risks
Regulating the pain clinics in the area

sc.title: Roseanna - discharge planning and Medicare
sc.text:
Henry Dodson, a social worker for a hospital, is working on care coordination for Roseanna, a 93-year-old patient discharging to a nursing facility after a hip fracture from a fall at home. Henry notices that Roseanna has Medicare insurance coverage. Roseanna has no living

relatives and lives alone in a one-story house. Henry believes that Roseanna will require a long-term stay in the nursing facility and is unsure that Roseanna will ever return to living at the home alone.

items.q: Roseanna is discharging to a skilled nursing facility. This is an example of which type of health care facility?
items.ex: A skilled nursing facility gives 24-hour nursing and rehabilitation and is a type of long-term care facility.
w: Roseanna is leaving the hospital, not entering one.
Hospice is for patients expected to die within 6 months.

alt.q: What does the skilled nursing facility Roseanna is entering provide?
alt.a: Nursing and rehab on a 24-hour basis
alt.ex: An SNF provides nursing and rehabilitation services around the clock.
w: Nursing supervision at least 8 hours a day
That's an intermediate nursing care facility.
Housing and meals but no daily nursing
Care only for those with under 6 months to live

alt.q: If Roseanna needed housing, meals, and help with daily living but no daily nursing, which long-term option would fit?
alt.ex: Assisted living offers housing, meals, and personal care without daily nursing.
w: That's a hospital unit before discharge.

sc.title: Roseanna - discharge planning and Medicare
sc.text:
Henry Dodson, a social worker for a hospital, is working on care coordination for Roseanna, a 93-year-old patient discharging to a nursing facility after a hip fracture from a fall at home. Henry notices that Roseanna has Medicare insurance coverage. Roseanna has no living

relatives and lives alone in a one-story house. Henry believes that Roseanna will require a long-term stay in the nursing facility and is unsure that Roseanna will ever return to living at the home alone.

items.q: Roseanna explains to Henry that a neighbor fell last month and credited their recovery to the use of acupuncture medicine. Henry knows that acupuncture is a form of complementary, alternative, or integrative medicine known as
items.ex: Acupuncture inserts tiny needles at specific points to relieve energy blocks and may be the oldest application of energy theories.
w: Massage therapy works by relaxing muscles by hand.
Homeopathy uses tiny doses of symptom-causing substances.
Osteopathy focuses on the musculoskeletal system.

alt.q: How is acupuncture believed to work?
alt.a: Needles relieve blocks in the body's energy
alt.ex: Acupuncture uses needles at specific points to relieve energy blocks.
w: Tiny doses of a substance trigger healing
Spine adjustments relieve pressure on nerves

alt.q: Which practice belongs to the same category as acupuncture?
alt.ex: Reiki, like acupuncture, is an energy therapy.

sc.title: Roseanna - discharge planning and Medicare
sc.text:
Henry Dodson, a social worker for a hospital, is working on care coordination for Roseanna, a 93-year-old patient discharging to a nursing facility after a hip fracture from a fall at home. Henry notices that Roseanna has Medicare insurance coverage. Roseanna has no living

relatives and lives alone in a one-story house. Henry believes that Roseanna will require a long-term stay in the nursing facility and is unsure that Roseanna will ever return to living at the home alone.

items.q: Based on the scenario, Roseanna is most likely being discharged from which hospital floor?
items.ex: A transitional care unit gives lower-level care while discharge plans, like Roseanna's move to a nursing facility, are made.
w: The ICU is for critically ill patients needing continuous care.
Roseanna is beyond surgery and is being prepared for discharge.
Cardiac care is for heart conditions.

alt.q: What is the purpose of the hospital unit Roseanna is most likely leaving?
alt.a: Lower-level care while discharge is planned
alt.ex: A TCU gives lower-level care while discharge plans are made.
w: Continuous care with 1 or 2 patients per nurse
Care for sudden conditions needing immediate help

alt.q: Henry is arranging Roseanna's move to a nursing facility while Roseanna is still in the hospital. Which unit best fits a patient at this stage?
alt.ex: Patients awaiting discharge plans are cared for in a TCU.
w: That's for sudden conditions on arrival.

items.q: A physical therapy assistant performs home visits for a rehabilitation service. One of their patients has rheumatoid arthritis and has asked the physical therapy assistant's opinion about taking Chinese herbal remedies they have read may improve the health of their joints. What is the best thing for the physical therapy assistant to do?
items.a: Tell the patient they should check with their physician about the herbs
items.ex: Herbal remedies may not be proven safe or effective and can affect treatment, so the patient should check with their physician.
w: Tell the patient they will find out more about the herbs and get back to them
Researching it alone leaves out the physician who manages the patient's care.
Advise the patient to avoid Chinese medicine, as it may cause more harm than good
A blanket warning against Chinese medicine isn't the PTA's role.
Tell the patient they should try the herbs and see how they work
Recommending an unproven remedy is outside the PTA's role.

alt.q: A patient asks a medical assistant whether a supplement advertised as a 'miracle cure' will help their arthritis. What is the best response?
alt.a: Suggest they ask their provider about it first
alt.ex: Health care workers should direct patients to their provider and reliable sources.
w: Tell them natural products are always safe
Tell them all supplements are dangerous fraud
Tell them to try it for a month and see what happens

alt.q: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis asks a physical therapy assistant about Chinese herbal remedies. Why should the PTA refer them to their physician?
alt.a: The herbs' safety and effects may be unproven
alt.ex: Many complementary therapies' safety and effectiveness are unproven.
w: Herbal remedies are illegal in the U.S.
Physicians are paid more to answer questions
PTAs may never discuss any health topic at all
PTAs talk with patients; they just shouldn't advise on herbs.

items.q: Alzheimer's disease can be cured if it is caught in the early stages.
items.ex: Alzheimer's disease is progressive and has no cure; it is the seventh leading cause of death.
items.ww: Early detection doesn't cure Alzheimer's; it is progressive and fatal.

alt.q: Alzheimer's disease is progressive and is one of the leading causes of death in the United States.
alt.ex: Alzheimer's is progressive and ranks seventh among causes of death.
alt.ww: It's progressive and the seventh leading cause of death.

alt.q: Alzheimer's disease accounts for only a small fraction of dementia cases.
alt.ex: Alzheimer's is the most common dementia, 60–80% of cases.
alt.ww: It accounts for 60–80% of dementia cases.

items.q: Antibiotic resistance is considered one of our most serious health threats.
items.ex: Bacteria mutate to resist antibiotics, causing about 2 million illnesses and 23,000 deaths a year, making it one of our most serious health threats.
items.ww: The text calls antibiotic resistance one of our most serious health threats.

alt.q: Antibiotic resistance is a minor problem that causes few illnesses each year.
alt.ex: It causes about 2 million illnesses and 23,000 deaths every year.
alt.ww: It's a serious threat with millions of illnesses.

alt.q: Antibiotic resistance develops when bacteria mutate so that drugs work less well or not at all.
alt.ex: Mutation reduces or eliminates antibiotics' effectiveness.

items.q: What theory did Margaret Newman develop after observing that even patients with incurable conditions could live meaningful lives?
items.ex: Margaret Newman, RN, developed the theory of expanding consciousness to help patients find meaning by focusing on possibilities rather than limitations.
w: Wellness is promoting health through prevention, not Newman's theory.
Psychosomatic refers to illness from mental factors.
Holistic medicine is a broader approach, not Newman's theory.

alt.q: What does the theory of expanding consciousness focus on?
alt.ex: Newman's theory helps patients make life meaningful despite incurable conditions.
w: Curing every disease a patient has
Treating symptoms with tiny natural doses

alt.q: Who developed the theory of expanding consciousness?
alt.ex: Newman, an RN, developed it after seeing patients live with incurable conditions.
w: Not the author of this theory.
Hippocrates, a Greek physician of ancient times
An ancient physician, not this theory's author.

items.q: What is the meaning of health disparities?
items.a: The differences in the health status of different groups of people
items.ex: Health disparities are differences in the health status of different groups of people.
w: The differences between different types of health facilities
That compares facilities, not the health of groups.
The types of health care paid for by insurance companies
The lack of access to health care experienced by low-income families
Lack of access contributes to disparities but isn't the definition.

alt.q: People in a neighborhood without grocery stores have higher rates of obesity and diabetes than people elsewhere. This is an example of:
alt.ex: A difference in health between groups is a health disparity.

alt.q: Which situation shows a health disparity?
alt.a: One group has shorter life expectancy than another
alt.ex: Health disparities are differences in health status between groups.
w: A hospital charges more than a nearby clinic
An insurer covers some drugs but not others
A patient sees three different specialists at once

items.q: Hospice care must be provided in a special facility called a hospice.
items.ex: Hospice care can be given in a hospice facility, another care facility, or the patient's own home.
items.ww: Hospice can also be provided in a care facility or the patient's home.

alt.q: A dying patient can receive hospice care in their own home.
alt.ex: Hospice may be provided at home, in a hospice, or in a care facility.
alt.ww: Home is one of the settings for hospice.

alt.q: Hospice care is available only in hospital intensive care units.
alt.ex: Hospice is given in a hospice facility, a care facility, or the home.
alt.ww: It's offered in several settings, not ICUs.

items.q: A primary care physician has referred a patient to an oncologist. Preliminary tests show that the patient may have colon cancer. The patient is 77 years old and is uncomfortable about visiting a physician they have never met. They are especially distraught about the possibility of having a life-threatening condition and do not understand why the doctor they have been seeing for many years cannot take care of the problem. What characteristic of modern health care is responsible for the referral to the oncologist?
items.ex: Specialization divides care among specialists like oncologists, so the primary care physician refers cancer care to one.
w: Insurance changes don't explain referring to a cancer specialist.
The increasing cost of primary care
Primary care costs aren't the reason for the referral.
Primary care physicians aren't restricted; cancer care is a specialty.

alt.q: A 77-year-old patient is upset at being referred to an oncologist they have never met instead of their longtime doctor. Which effect of specialization does this show?
alt.a: Long-term provider relationships are breaking down
alt.ex: Specialization means one trusted provider no longer gives most of a patient's care.
w: Patients see fewer providers than in the past
Health care has become much less expensive
Each patient now receives all care from one trusted doctor

alt.q: A 77-year-old patient referred to a new oncologist feels uneasy seeing a physician they have never met. What can the medical assistant in that office do to help most?
alt.a: Help them understand and trust their new care
alt.ex: Specialization increases the need for caring attitudes and good communication.
w: Tell them to return to their former physician
That doesn't help them get needed care.
Avoid talking so the oncologist explains everything
Choose another specialist for them to see

items.q: At the beginning of the 20th century, the major causes of death were ______.
items.ex: Early in the 1900s, infectious diseases, especially influenza and pneumonia, were the major killers.
w: Cancer and stroke became leading causes later.
Cancer and heart disease are leading causes today.
Work-related accidents were not the major killers.

alt.q: Which type of illness caused the most deaths in the U.S. around 1900?
alt.ex: Influenza, pneumonia, and other infections were the major killers then.

alt.q: Why are influenza and pneumonia no longer the leading killers they were in 1900?
alt.ex: Penicillin, antibiotics, and immunizations brought many infections under control.
w: Hospitals began keeping patients for months
Most people moved out of large cities

items.q: Which of the following services provided in the patient's home would be considered medically necessary for insurance reimbursement?
items.ex: Giving IV medications is a skilled, medically related service; nonmedical help like cooking and cleaning usually isn't covered.
w: Providing personal hygiene, such as bathing
Bathing is personal care, not a skilled medical service.
Cooking is nonmedical help that usually isn't covered.
House cleaning to maintain safe conditions
House cleaning is nonmedical help that usually isn't covered.

alt.q: Which home service is LEAST likely to be paid for by Medicare?
alt.ex: Nonmedical help such as shopping, cooking, and cleaning usually isn't covered.
w: Checking the healing of a wound

alt.q: Medicare pays for medically related home health services only when the homebound patient:
alt.a: Is expected to improve and recover
alt.ex: Coverage requires that the homebound person is expected to improve.
w: Has no family who can help at home
Has lived alone for at least a year
Is expected to die within six months

items.q: The principal purpose of the National Institutes of Health is to _______.
items.ex: The NIH's 27 institutes and centers conduct and support medical research.
w: ensure that prescription drugs are safe
Ensuring drug safety is the FDA's job.
Collecting statistics is done by health departments, not the NIH's main purpose.
control the spread of infectious diseases
Controlling disease spread is the CDC's job.

alt.q: A scientist gets federal funding to study a new cancer treatment. Which agency most likely provides it?
alt.ex: The NIH conducts and supports medical research.

alt.q: Which agency is matched with its correct role?
alt.ex: The NIH's role is medical research.

items.q: One concern of the federal government is that some nursing homes in the United States sacrifice quality for profit.
items.ex: For-profit nursing facilities have been accused of inadequate care, and the federal government raised its rating standards in 2015.
items.ww: The text describes concern that for-profit facilities put profits over care.

alt.q: In 2015, about 21% of nursing homes received deficiencies for serious quality violations.
alt.ex: After standards were raised, 21% had serious deficiencies.
alt.ww: The text reports 21% had serious deficiencies.

alt.q: Federal officials have found no quality problems in for-profit nursing homes.
alt.ex: For-profit facilities have been accused of inadequate care, and 21% of homes had serious deficiencies in 2015.

items.q: A beneficial health care practice recognized by many conventional health care providers is
items.ex: Massage therapy is widely recognized as beneficial because it relaxes muscles, improves circulation, speeds healing, and relieves pain.
w: Reiki is an energy therapy that isn't widely accepted.
Use of magnets to relieve pain
Magnet therapy isn't recognized as effective.

alt.q: Which benefits of massage therapy are widely recognized?
alt.ex: Massage relaxes muscles, improving circulation, healing, and pain relief.
w: Correction of poor vision and hearing

alt.q: A patient recovering from a sports injury asks which complementary practice most providers accept as helpful. Which is best?
alt.ex: Massage is widely recognized as beneficial by conventional providers.

items.q: The major reason that infectious diseases are mostly under control today is because of the ______.
items.ex: Penicillin and other antibiotics, along with immunizations, made many infectious diseases almost unheard of.
w: improvement of personal health habits among the general population
Personal habits help but aren't the major reason given.
discovery of what causes these diseases
Knowing the cause didn't by itself control the diseases.
increase in the number of health care providers to treat these diseases
More providers isn't the reason given.

alt.q: Which 20th-century advance did the most to bring infections like pneumonia under control?
alt.ex: Antibiotics, with immunizations, brought infectious diseases under control.

alt.q: Why do physicians today rarely see patients dying of infections that were common in 1900?
alt.a: Antibiotics can now treat these infections
alt.ex: Penicillin and antibiotics made many infections treatable.
w: Germs that caused them have died out
People today have stronger natural immunity
Hospitals now isolate every sick person

items.q: Which section of a hospital is for patients with serious illnesses or injuries that require the use of special equipment and continuous monitoring and nursing care?
items.ex: The ICU serves seriously ill or injured patients who need special equipment and continuous monitoring, with one or two patients per nurse.
w: The emergency department handles sudden conditions needing immediate care.
A trauma center gives comprehensive care for life-threatening injuries on arrival.
The surgical floor cares for patients before and after surgery.

alt.q: A patient on a ventilator needs constant monitoring and one nurse for every one or two patients. Where are they most likely placed?
alt.ex: The ICU provides continuous care with special equipment.
w: That's for conditions like infections and diabetes.
That's for patients less critical than ICU patients.

alt.q: Which describes the intensive care unit?
alt.a: Continuous care, one or two patients per nurse
alt.ex: ICU patients get continuous care and monitoring.
w: Lower-level care while discharge plans are made
Care for infections and diabetes on a general floor
Sudden conditions treated as soon as patients arrive

items.q: Medicine made great advances in preventive medicine in the 20th century.
items.ex: Life expectancy rose from 47 in 1900 to 70 in 1950 mainly because of preventive measures like vaccination, pasteurization, and sanitation.
items.ww: The text credits 20th-century gains mostly to preventive measures.

alt.q: The rise in life expectancy from 1900 to 1950 was due mainly to new cures such as organ transplants.
alt.ex: It was due mainly to preventive measures like vaccination, pasteurization, asepsis, and sanitation.
alt.ww: Prevention, not cures, drove the gains.

alt.q: Vaccination and sanitation helped life expectancy rise from 47 to 70 years in the first half of the 20th century.
alt.ex: Preventive measures drove the increase.

items.q: With the increasing division of health care provided by various health care providers, the cost of health care has increased.
items.ex: Specialization divided care among many providers, and the text lists the increased cost of health care as one effect.
items.ww: The text lists higher costs as an effect of specialization.

alt.q: Specialization has made health care less expensive because each provider focuses on one area.
alt.ex: Specialization has increased the cost of health care.

alt.q: One effect of specialization is that long-term provider–patient relationships are breaking down.
alt.ex: Patients now get care from many providers they may not know.

items.q: Which of the following is an example of alternative medicine?
items.a: Using acupuncture instead of surgery to treat back pain
items.ex: Alternative medicine is used instead of Western medicine, as when acupuncture replaces surgery.
w: A patient receiving chemotherapy for cancer is prescribed meditation and nutritional supplements to manage symptoms and side effects
That's integrative medicine: a provider combines Western and complementary care.
Personalized medicine is gene-based Western care.
Using meditation along with medication to lower blood pressure
Using meditation along with medication is complementary medicine.

alt.q: A patient uses meditation together with prescribed blood pressure medicine. What is this called?
alt.ex: Complementary methods are used together with Western medicine.
w: That's used instead of Western care.

alt.q: What distinguishes alternative medicine from complementary medicine?
alt.a: It's used instead of Western medicine
alt.ex: Alternative practices replace Western medicine; complementary ones are added to it.
w: It's used along with Western medicine
It's based on each patient's genes
It's offered only by MDs in hospitals

items.q: Which of the following is NOT a type of long-term care?
items.ex: A transitional care unit is a hospital unit for lower-level care while discharge plans are made, not a long-term care setting.
w: Assisted living is a type of long-term care.
An intermediate nursing care facility is long-term care.
A skilled nursing facility is long-term care.

alt.q: Which of these is a type of long-term care?
alt.ex: Adult foster homes give 24-hour care to a few residents long term.

alt.q: Where is a transitional care unit found?
alt.ex: A TCU is a hospital unit giving lower-level care before discharge.

items.q: As a result of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act of 2010, every American can now afford to pay for health insurance and medical care.
items.ex: Insurance can still be expensive with high deductibles, and about one-third of the middle class reportedly can't afford them.
items.ww: Many still can't afford deductibles; parts of the law were also repealed.

alt.q: Even after the Affordable Care Act, some Americans struggle to pay their insurance deductibles.
alt.ex: Deductibles can be several thousand dollars, and one-third of the middle class reportedly can't afford them.

alt.q: Because of the Affordable Care Act, part-time workers without employer insurance no longer have trouble affording coverage.
alt.ex: The text says this group especially struggles to afford coverage.
alt.ww: This group is among those who struggle most.

items.q: It is estimated that as many as ____ of patients do not take their prescription medications as directed.
items.ex: As many as 50% of patients don't take their prescriptions as directed, which is why medication adherence matters.

alt.q: About what fraction of patients may not take their prescriptions as directed?
alt.ex: Up to 50% of patients don't take medications as directed.

alt.q: Medication adherence means taking medicine correctly. Up to what share of patients fail to do this?
alt.ex: As many as half of patients don't take prescriptions as directed.

items.q: One reason for racism in the treatment of patients is because of false beliefs about biological differences between Blacks and Whites.

sc.title: Two health care workers after a car accident
sc.text:
>> Several years ago, I was involved in a terrible car accident. With my injuries, I was hospitalized for several weeks. Throughout the process, I had two very different experiences with two particular health care professionals. The first health care worker never talked to me,

seemed annoyed that she had to help me, and once I had to confirm that she was giving me the correct medication dosage. It was a good thing, too, because she hadn't taken the time to check the chart for changes to my prescription. It was awful because I felt so on edge whenever she was around. One day, I heard her talking about me to another staff member out in the hall. I mean, that's a violation of my HIPAA rights. I was mortified, and that was the last time I asked her any questions about my health or treatment. The other experience I had was polar opposite. The second worker was always cheerful and gave me his full attention when he came in the room. He gave me the impression that he was a professional and even caught an error on my chart. He valued confidentiality, so I felt like I could talk to him about concerns I had, and that was good because there were things that needed to be addressed. It was a relief to interact with a health care worker like that because I could just focus on getting well. I made a point of letting the supervisor know about both of my experiences.
