The visit forms an implied contract; the arm gesture shows consent.

alt.q: Which is an example of implied consent?
alt.a: Opening the mouth for a dental injection
alt.ex: Consent shown by an action is implied consent.
w: Agreeing out loud after a full explanation

alt.q: How does implied consent differ from express consent?
alt.a: It's shown by actions, not formal words
alt.ex: Express consent is given directly; implied consent is shown by actions.
w: It's given only by a court
It's required for every invasive procedure

items.q: A company submits a claim to Medicare for a wheelchair for which the customer did not qualify. Which of the following terms describes this action?
items.ex: Submitting claims for services or equipment a patient doesn't qualify for is health care fraud.
w: No contract with the customer was broken.
Incompetence is lack of skill, not dishonest billing.

alt.q: Which is an example of health care fraud?
alt.ex: Claims for services not performed are fraud.

alt.q: What is fraud?
alt.a: Dishonesty that involves cheating or trickery
alt.ex: Fraud is dishonesty through cheating or trickery.
w: Failing to meet the standard of care
Holding a patient against their own will at a facility

items.q: The Patient Care Partnership is a standard form that health care providers use to create written contracts with patients.
items.ex: The Patient Care Partnership is an AHA document explaining what patients can expect and their rights and responsibilities during a hospital stay.
items.ww: It's a statement of expectations, rights, and responsibilities, not a contract form.

alt.q: The Patient Care Partnership replaced the Patient's Bill of Rights that the American Hospital Association developed in 1973.
alt.ex: The AHA updated and renamed its 1973 Patient's Bill of Rights.
alt.ww: It's the renamed Bill of Rights.

alt.q: The Patient Care Partnership is a federal law that requires patients to sign treatment contracts.
alt.ex: It's an AHA statement of what patients can expect, not a law or contract.
alt.ww: It isn't a law or a contract.

items.q: A patient had hip surgery at a large hospital. They met with the surgeon prior to the procedure, who explained the procedure, answered the patient's questions, and asked them to sign some forms. What term describes the formalized promises made to Robin?
items.ex: When a procedure is discussed in detail and the patient agrees and signs, the formalized promises form an express contract.
w: Good Samaritan laws protect emergency volunteers.
Informed consent is the permission process; the formalized promises are an express contract.
Implied consent is shown by actions, not discussion and forms.

alt.q: How does an express contract differ from an implied contract?
alt.a: It's discussed in detail and agreed to
alt.ex: Express contracts are discussed in detail; implied ones come from actions.
w: It's created only by the patient's actions
It needs no consideration or exchange
It can only be made in an emergency

alt.q: Which situation creates an express contract?
alt.a: A surgeon explains surgery and the patient signs
alt.ex: Detailed discussion plus agreement forms an express contract.
w: A patient visits a clinic and later pays the bill
A patient holds out an arm for a cuff
A bystander gives CPR at a game

items.q: Which of the following illustrates a situation where a release of patient information would be legal?
items.a: The patient's injuries are life-threatening and caused by a shooting.
items.ex: Patient information can't be released without written approval except for disclosures allowed or required by law, such as life-threatening injuries caused by violence.
w: The patient's sister wants to know details about his condition before traveling to visit.
Relatives need the patient's written approval.
The patient is being cared for at a hospital supported by public funds. A newspaper reporter asks for information.
Public funding doesn't allow release to reporters.
The patient is younger than age 21.
Age 21 isn't a basis for release.

alt.q: Which person may receive a patient's information without written approval?
alt.a: An official receiving a required abuse report
alt.ex: Only those allowed or required by law, like abuse reports, may receive it.
w: The patient's close friend who asks
A relative who calls the hospital asking about them

alt.q: A patient tells a nurse they plan to end their life after discharge. What must the nurse do?
alt.ex: Confidences must be revealed when serious harm is likely.
w: Report to the provider or supervisor.
Wait until discharge to see what happens

items.q: A respiratory therapist who works at a children's hospital is careful to keep their technical knowledge and skills up-to-date. What ethical principle is illustrated by their actions?
items.ex: Keeping knowledge and skills up to date is listed under 'do no harm' in Table 4–2.
w: Justice is fairness and equal treatment.
Keeping promises is following through on commitments.
Autonomy is the patient's right to decide.

alt.q: Which action is also part of 'do no harm'?
alt.a: Working within your scope of practice
alt.ex: Staying within your scope of practice prevents harm.
w: Treating all patients equally regardless of background

alt.q: A dental assistant renews their CPR certification before it expires. Which principle does this support?
alt.ex: Keeping certifications current is part of 'do no harm.'

items.q: One of the dental assistants employed in a large dental practice caused an injury to a patient while preparing the patient for a procedure. Which legal concept can be used to describe the dentist's responsibility for the actions of the dental assistant?
items.ex: Respondeat superior makes employers, like the dentist, liable for their employees' actions.
w: Informed consent is the patient's permission.
Damages are the money awarded, not the responsibility.

alt.q: A front desk worker promises a patient 'you won't have any trouble,' and the surgeon is later sued. Why can the surgeon be liable?
alt.a: The worker acted as the surgeon's agent
alt.ex: Employees are agents of the professionals they work for.
w: The worker was not trained in surgery
The patient had no consent form

alt.q: What is an agent in health care law?
alt.a: Someone authorized to act for another
alt.ex: Health care workers act as agents of their employers.
w: A lawyer hired by the patient

items.q: What can a health care professional learn from their profession's code of ethics?
items.a: Guidelines of right and wrong conduct for their profession
items.ex: A code of ethics gives guidelines of right and wrong conduct for members of a profession.
w: Federal laws aren't in a code of ethics.
Laws governing a profession come from legislatures.
Duties they can and cannot legally perform
Legal duties are set by scope-of-practice laws.

alt.q: A new surgical technologist wants to know the standards of right conduct expected of them. Where should they look?
alt.ex: Each profession's code sets standards of conduct.

alt.q: Which is true about professional codes of ethics?
alt.a: They set standards of conduct for a field
alt.ex: Codes set standards of professional conduct.
w: They are federal laws with prison terms
They list duties legally allowed to perform
They are written by each patient

items.q: The policies created by the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) are designed to ________.
items.a: protect the privacy of patient medical records
items.ex: HIPAA set national standards to protect the privacy of patients' health information.
w: provide funding for expanded health insurance for low-income individuals
control the rising cost of health care
ensure that patients are fully informed about possible outcomes of treatments
Informing patients about outcomes is informed consent.

alt.q: When was HIPAA passed?
alt.ex: HIPAA was passed in 1996 and implemented in 2003.

alt.q: Why was HIPAA's privacy standard considered important?
alt.ex: Many feared electronic records could compromise patient privacy.
w: Paper records cost too much to store
Insurers wanted to sell patient data to employers

items.q: A home health aide suspects that her older adult client is being abused by the client's niece. What should they do?
items.a: Report the signs or symptoms of abuse to their supervisor
items.ex: Suspected elder abuse should be reported to the supervisor; health professionals have an ethical duty to report.
w: Report through the supervisor rather than calling police directly.
Ask the client if they are being abused
Asking the client directly isn't the reporting step and may put them at risk.

alt.q: Which agency investigates elder abuse in most areas?
alt.ex: Adult Protective Services is a main agency for elder abuse.

alt.q: Which sign might make a home health aide suspect an older client is being financially abused?
alt.a: Money missing from the client's account
alt.ex: Taking financial resources is a form of elder abuse.
w: The client enjoys visits from family
The client wants to live alone
The client's niece helps with grocery shopping

items.q: Which of the following is the best example of the principle "Be Discreet"?
items.a: Do not leave patient records where others can see them
items.ex: Keeping records out of others' view protects patient privacy, which is being discreet.
w: Admit your mistakes and work to correct them
Learn the rules for reporting suspected child abuse
Abuse reporting rules fall under upholding justice.

alt.q: Which action shows 'be discreet'?
alt.a: Closing the curtain before an exam
alt.ex: Protecting physical privacy is part of being discreet.
w: Admitting a mistake to a supervisor
Treating every patient the same way

alt.q: Which action would violate 'be discreet'?
alt.a: Talking about a patient in an elevator
alt.ex: Patients shouldn't be discussed in public places.
w: Charting care accurately and on time
Explaining a procedure to the patient
Asking the patient to sign a release form

items.q: Denise is a member of a political organization. The organization has a reputation for holding political rallies that include hate speech. The group wants to rent a local high school stadium for a large rally. The school district refuses due to the reputation of the group. The group objects, stating they have a right to free speech. Which term below can be used to describe this situation?
items.ex: Hate speech on public grounds pits free speech against equal treatment, an ethical dilemma with no clear answer.
w: A code of ethics is a professional document.

alt.q: A group known for hate speech is refused use of a public school stadium and claims a right to free speech. Which values conflict?
alt.a: Free speech vs. equal treatment for all
alt.ex: Table 4–1 lists this conflict for hate speech on public grounds.
w: Gun rights vs. protecting the public
An eye for an eye vs. do not kill
Patient privacy vs. the public's right to know

alt.q: Which is an example of an ethical dilemma listed in Table 4–1?
alt.ex: Capital punishment is a Table 4–1 dilemma.

items.q: A respiratory therapist's supervisor is in a hurry and asks them to perform a procedure that they have not been trained to do. What should they do?
items.a: Tell their supervisor that they do not have the training and cannot do the procedure
items.ex: Working within your scope of practice is part of 'do no harm,' so the therapist should decline a procedure they aren't trained for.
w: Do the procedure to the best of their ability
Doing an untrained procedure risks harm.
Ask a coworker to help them with the procedure
A coworker's help doesn't make it within their training.
Not do the procedure but report that it has been done
Reporting an undone procedure as done is fraud.

alt.q: A respiratory therapist refuses to perform a procedure they haven't been trained to do. Which principle are they following?
alt.ex: Working within your scope of practice is 'do no harm.'

alt.q: A therapist performs a procedure they weren't trained for, and the patient is hurt. What could the therapist be charged with?
alt.ex: Failing to meet the expected standard of care is negligence.

items.q: Two friends who work as registered nurses in an emergency department are at a college football game when a man sitting near them appears to be having a heart attack. Why can they volunteer to assist without being concerned about liability?
items.ex: Good Samaritan laws protect people who volunteer emergency care from liability unless they cause harm intentionally or through extreme carelessness.
w: The Patient Care Partnership covers hospital patients' expectations.
The Hippocratic Oath is a physicians' ethics oath.

alt.q: Two off-duty nurses help a fan having a heart attack at a game. What should they avoid while helping?
alt.ex: Volunteers shouldn't go beyond their scope of training.
w: Staying with the man until help comes

alt.q: Which situation is protected by Good Samaritan laws?
alt.a: A hiker giving first aid to a fallen stranger
alt.ex: The laws protect volunteers in emergencies.
w: A paid nurse making an error on duty
An ED nurse injuring a patient during a shift

items.q: New federal health care laws that were created in 2010 say that a person can no longer be denied coverage because of preexisting medical conditions and that certain preventative health screenings must be provided without extra charge. Which of the following includes these laws?
items.ex: The 2010 Affordable Care Act includes protections like no denial for preexisting conditions and free preventive screenings.
w: A code of ethics is a professional document.
The Hippocratic Oath is an ancient physicians' oath.

alt.q: Under the ACA Patient's Bill of Rights, until what age can an eligible young adult stay on a parent's plan?
alt.ex: Young adults meeting requirements can stay on a parent's plan until 26.

alt.q: Which protection is part of the Affordable Care Act's Patient's Bill of Rights?
alt.a: 30 days' notice before coverage is canceled
alt.ex: Insurers must give 30 days' notice before canceling coverage.
w: Unlimited cash payments for all medical bills

items.q: Which term means the disclosure of unauthorized information about a person that can harm that person's reputation?
items.ex: Defamation of character is disclosing unauthorized information that harms a person's reputation; it can be libel (written) or slander (spoken).
w: False imprisonment is holding someone against their will.
Breach of contract is failing to fulfill an agreement.

alt.q: A lab tech tells a friend that an acquaintance tested positive for HIV. What could they be charged with?
alt.ex: Spoken defamation is slander.

alt.q: Libel and slander are both forms of:
alt.ex: Both harm a person's reputation.

items.q: A patient has terminal lung cancer. Their family understands that there is no cure. They signed a document that includes their wish to not have CPR administered. This document is called a(n) _____.
items.ex: A living will states the type and extent of care a person wants, such as no CPR.
w: The Patient Self-Determination Act is a law, not a document a patient signs.
durable power of attorney for health care
A durable power of attorney names a decision-maker.
Informed consent is permission for a specific treatment.

alt.q: How does a living will differ from a durable power of attorney for health care?
alt.a: It lists wishes instead of naming a person
alt.ex: A living will states care wishes; a durable power of attorney names a decision-maker.
w: It names a person rather than stating wishes
It applies only after the patient has died
It is signed by the physician, not the patient

alt.q: A patient wants to record in advance that they don't want a ventilator if they become terminally ill. Which document fits?
alt.ex: A living will states the type and extent of care wanted.

items.q: A pharmacist makes an error when filling a prescription because they are not paying full attention to their work. Which of the following words applies to this situation?
items.ex: Negligence is failing to give the standard of care expected from someone with that training, such as a careless dispensing error.
w: Damages are money awarded for an injury.

alt.q: Which professional is held to the highest standard of care?
alt.ex: More training means a higher standard of care.

alt.q: Which action helps a pharmacist prevent negligence?
alt.ex: Checking medications three times helps prevent errors.
w: Relying on memory instead of the label

items.q: What is the common name for a drug assigned by the United States Adopted Name Council?
items.ex: The generic name is the drug's common name, assigned by the United States Adopted Name Council.
w: The chemical name is the drug's molecular formula.
The trade name is the brand name.
The official name is the U.S. Pharmacopeia/National Formulary listing.

alt.q: Acetaminophen is the name the United States Adopted Name Council gave to the drug sold as Tylenol. Which type of drug name is acetaminophen?
alt.ex: Acetaminophen is the common (generic) name; Tylenol is the trade name.

alt.q: Which group assigns a drug's generic (common) name?
alt.ex: The United States Adopted Name Council assigns the generic name.
w: The FDA approves drugs; the text credits the Council.
The text credits the Council, not the maker.

items.q: Which of the following letters is a combining vowel?
items.ex: The combining vowel, usually 'o', links a word root to another word part, as in cardi/o.
w: Not the combining vowel; the text's combining vowel is o.
Not the combining vowel; the text's combining vowel is o.
Not the combining vowel; the text's combining vowel is o.

alt.q: In the combining form gastr/o, what is the letter after the slash?
alt.ex: The 'o' in gastr/o is the combining vowel that joins the root to other word parts.
w: Prefixes go at the beginning of a term.
It is part of the word root
The root is gastr; the o is added to it.

alt.q: Which letter is most often added to a word root to create a combining form?
alt.ex: Adding 'o' to a root (cardi + o = cardi/o) creates a combining form.

items.q: What are word parts that are attached to the end of word roots and combining forms to add to or change their meaning?
items.ex: Suffixes are attached to the end of word roots and combining forms to add to or change their meaning.
w: Word roots give the main meaning.
A combining form is a root plus a vowel.

alt.q: In the term 'appendicitis,' what kind of word part is '-itis'?
alt.ex: -itis sits at the end of the term and adds the meaning 'inflammation,' so it is a suffix.
w: That's a root plus a vowel.

alt.q: Which statement about suffixes is accurate?
alt.a: They attach to the end of a root
alt.ex: Suffixes are added at the end of word roots and combining forms.
w: They attach to the start of a root
They give a term its main meaning
They are the vowel joining roots

items.q: What are word parts that are attached to the beginning of word roots and combining forms to add to or change their meaning?
items.ex: Prefixes are attached to the beginning of word roots and combining forms to add to or change their meaning.
w: A combining form is a root plus a vowel.
Word roots give the main meaning.

alt.q: In 'bradycardia,' the part 'brady-' is which type of word part?
alt.ex: brady- is attached to the beginning of the term and means slow, so it is a prefix.
w: Suffixes are at the end, like -ia.

alt.q: What do word parts such as hypo-, inter-, and post- have in common?
alt.a: They attach at the start of a term
alt.ex: These are prefixes, which are attached to the beginning of roots and combining forms.
w: They are added at the very end of a term
They give a term its main meaning
That is the word root's job.
They link two word roots together

items.q: What everyday word means observable or measurable evidence of a patient's condition?
items.ex: In medical language, a sign is observable or measurable evidence of a patient's condition.
w: An everyday word, but not the term for evidence of a condition.
Acute means it comes on quickly and needs urgent care.

alt.q: A patient's blood pressure reading of 180/110 is measurable evidence of their condition. In medical language, this is called a
alt.ex: Observable or measurable evidence of a condition, like a blood pressure reading, is a sign.
w: Acute describes quick onset needing urgent care.
A symptom is what the patient reports feeling.

alt.q: In medical language, what does the everyday word 'sign' mean?
alt.ex: A sign is observable or measurable evidence of a patient's condition.
w: A condition that develops very quickly
A tumor that is not malignant or harmful
A feeling that the patient describes
That is a symptom, not a sign.

items.q: Which of the following is not one of the five tools listed in the text that are used to help students become proficient in medical terminology?
items.a: Discuss terminology with the instructor after class.
items.ex: The text's suggestions include studying a few words daily, practicing word parts in new combinations, and learning new terms from textbooks, but not discussing terms with the instructor after class.
w: As word parts are learned, practice using them in new combinations.
Listed: practice word parts in new combinations.
Learn new medical terms as they appear in this and other textbooks.
Listed: learn new terms as they appear in textbooks.
Study a few words each day. Avoid learning the entire list at the last minute.
Listed: study a few words each day.

alt.q: Which is one of the text's suggestions for becoming proficient in medical terminology?
alt.a: Practice written and spoken forms often
alt.ex: The text advises practicing both the written and spoken forms as much as possible.
w: Memorize full term lists the night before
The text says avoid last-minute learning.
Learn only terms your instructor assigns
The text says learn terms in this and other textbooks.
The text says accept help from coworkers.

alt.q: A student wants to follow the text's advice for learning medical terms. Which plan does NOT match that advice?
alt.a: Cram the full list right before the test
alt.ex: The text says to study a few words each day and avoid learning entire lists at the last minute.
w: Use a dictionary when unsure of spelling
This is one of the suggestions.
Combine learned word parts in new ways
This is one of the suggestions.
This is one of the suggestions.

items.q: What is the study of diseases and abnormal conditions?
items.ex: Pathophysiology is the study of diseases and abnormal conditions.
w: Pharmacology is the study of therapeutic drugs.
Etymology is the study of word origins.
Radiology deals with imaging such as x-rays.

alt.q: What does the subject pathophysiology cover?
alt.ex: Pathophysiology is the study of diseases and abnormal conditions.
w: Normal function of the body systems
Structure of the body and its parts

alt.q: Which pairing of subject and focus is correct?
alt.ex: Pathophysiology focuses on diseases and abnormal conditions.
w: Anatomy is structure; physiology is function.

items.q: What is the brand name for a drug assigned by the United States Adopted Name Council?
items.ex: The trade name is the drug's brand name, such as Tylenol. Note: the text says the United States Adopted Name Council assigns the generic (common) name, not the brand name.
w: The chemical name is the molecular formula.
The generic name is the common name from the Council.
The official name is the U.S. Pharmacopeia/National Formulary listing.

alt.q: Tylenol is which of the four types of drug names?
alt.ex: Tylenol is a brand name, which is the trade name.

alt.q: A drug's trade name is the same thing as its
alt.ex: The trade name is the brand name the drug is sold under, such as Tylenol.
w: The generic name is the common name.
That is usually the same as the generic name.

items.q: What everyday word describes a condition that comes on quickly, progresses rapidly, and requires urgent care?
items.ex: Acute describes a condition that comes on quickly, progresses rapidly, and requires urgent care.
w: An everyday word, but not the text's special term for quick onset.
A sign is observable or measurable evidence.

alt.q: A patient develops severe chest pain within minutes and needs immediate care. Which medical word best describes this condition?
alt.ex: A condition that comes on quickly, progresses rapidly, and needs urgent care is acute.

alt.q: In medical language, what does 'acute' mean?
alt.a: Comes on quickly and needs urgent care
alt.ex: Acute describes a condition that comes on quickly, progresses rapidly, and requires urgent care.
w: Develops slowly over many months or years
Not malignant and not likely to spread
Observable or measurable evidence of illness

items.q: Which of the following explains why it is important for health care professionals to be fluent in medical terminology?
items.a: There is less chance for confusion and error.
items.ex: Using exact medical language adds precision to communication and reduces the chance of confusion and error.
w: There is an increased risk patients will not benefit.
Fluency helps patients; it doesn't raise risk.
There is a decreased chance for professionals to be sued.
Not the reason the text gives.
There is an increased risk for confusion and error.
Fluency lowers, not raises, confusion and error.

alt.q: A health care professional who misuses medical terms or abbreviations is most likely to cause
alt.ex: Misunderstood words or abbreviations can lead to confusion and even harmful treatment.

alt.q: What is the main benefit of using medical terminology precisely?
alt.ex: Exact language adds precision to communication and lowers the chance of confusion and error.
w: It replaces the need to chart
Terms are used in charting, not instead of it.

items.q: Abbreviations formed by groups of letters taken from the first letter of a phrase are called
items.ex: Acronyms are abbreviations made of groups of letters taken from the first letters of a phrase, such as MRI (magnetic resonance image) and LASER.
w: Prefixes are word parts at the start of a term.
Suffixes are word parts at the end of a term.
Synonyms are words with the same meaning.

alt.q: MRI, ACL, and LASER are all examples of
alt.ex: Each is formed from the first letters of a phrase, such as magnetic resonance image.
w: Symbols are marks like ↑ or Δ.
Combining forms are roots plus a vowel.

alt.q: Which abbreviation is an acronym built from the first letter of each word in a phrase?
alt.ex: ACL comes from the first letters of anterior cruciate ligament, so it is an acronym.

items.q: What includes learning not only medical terms but also the associated abbreviations and symbols?
items.ex: Medical terminology includes not only medical terms but also their abbreviations and symbols.
w: Not the name the text uses for this.
Anatomy and physiology are body structure and function.
Close in meaning, but the text's term is medical terminology.

alt.q: Besides medical terms, the study of medical terminology also includes learning
alt.ex: Medical terminology covers terms plus their associated abbreviations and symbols.
w: Exams are clinical skills, not terminology.

alt.q: A student learning medical terms, abbreviations, and symbols is studying
alt.ex: Medical terminology includes terms along with their abbreviations and symbols.
w: Those cover body structure and function.
That is the study of disease.

items.q: What is the part of the medical term that gives the main meaning?
items.ex: The word root is the part of a medical term that gives its main meaning.
w: A prefix changes the meaning at the beginning.
A combining form is a root plus a vowel.
A suffix changes the meaning at the end.

alt.q: In the term 'gastritis,' which part carries the main meaning?
alt.ex: gastr is the word root and gives the main meaning, stomach.
w: There is no o in gastritis.
gastr is a root, not a prefix.

alt.q: In 'cardiology,' the part 'cardi' gives the term its main meaning. What is this part called?
alt.ex: The word root (cardi = heart) gives the main meaning of the term.
w: Prefixes go at the beginning to modify meaning.

items.q: Which of the following can misspelled words lead to?
items.ex: Similar-looking words can mean very different things, so misspellings can lead to treatment and medication errors.
w: Misspellings hinder mastery; they don't lead to it.
Too vague; the text names treatment and medication errors.
Misspellings don't teach new word parts.

alt.q: A nurse writes 'ileum' when 'ilium' was meant. What is the biggest risk of this misspelling?
alt.ex: Ilium (hip bone) and ileum (small intestine) are different body parts, so the error can lead to wrong treatment.
w: Only a minor cosmetic chart problem
Faster chart review by other staff

alt.q: Why does the text stress careful spelling of medical terms?
alt.a: Misspelled terms can cause care errors
alt.ex: Similar-looking terms can mean very different things, so misspellings can cause treatment and medication errors.
w: Patients grade staff on their spelling
Only Latin terms must be spelled right
All terms must be spelled correctly.

items.q: What is the name for medical terms that identify diseases, body structures, and procedures that are named for the person who identified or discovered them?
items.ex: Eponyms are terms for diseases, structures, and procedures named for the person who identified or discovered them.
w: Too broad; that's the whole language of medicine.
The text uses this for everyday words like 'sign.'

alt.q: The Heimlich maneuver and Hodgkin's disease are named for people. Terms like these are called
alt.ex: Terms named for the person who identified or discovered them are eponyms.
w: Acronyms come from first letters of a phrase.

alt.q: Which statement describes an eponym?
alt.a: A term named after a person
alt.ex: Eponyms name diseases, structures, or procedures after the person who identified or discovered them.
w: A term made from first letters
A term built from Greek roots
That is a term built from word parts.
A term with a special meaning

items.q: What is a valuable resource not only when taking health care courses but also as a handy reference in the work setting?
items.ex: A medical dictionary is useful while studying and as a handy reference at work for spelling, pronunciation, and meaning.
w: Records document patient care; they don't define terms.
Helpful, but not the resource the text names.
Not the resource the text names.

alt.q: A new medical assistant at work is unsure how to spell and pronounce a term. Which resource does the text recommend?
alt.ex: The text says to use a medical dictionary when unsure how to spell or pronounce a word.
w: Charts document care; they don't define terms.
Texting abbreviations should never be used.

alt.q: When choosing a medical dictionary, which feature does the text stress?
alt.a: Coverage of terms in your field
alt.ex: Check that the dictionary covers the terms used in your occupational area.
w: A foreword by a celebrity doctor
Pictures on every page of the book
Terms from a single language only

items.q: Which of the following is an example of an eponym?
items.ex: Alzheimer's disease is named for the person who identified it, so it is an eponym.

alt.q: Which of these terms is NOT an eponym?
alt.ex: Gastroenterology is built from word parts, not named after a person.

alt.q: Which eponym from the text names a medical treatment rather than a disease?
alt.ex: The text gives the Heimlich maneuver as an eponym for a treatment; Alzheimer's disease, Hodgkin's disease, and Munchausen syndrome are its disease examples.
w: The text lists it as a disease eponym.
The text lists it as a disease eponym.
The text lists it as a disease eponym.

sc.title: Cardiomyopathy terminology
sc.text: Alvin Boardman is a Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine (DO) working in a primary care clinic. Dr. Boardman is telling a patient, Martin, that recent tests show a new diagnosis of a cardiomyopathy, and Martin will require more testing to determine the most appropriate treatment plan.

items.q: The combining form "cardi/o" refers to which body part?
items.ex: cardi/o is the combining form for heart, the organ affected in cardiomyopathy.

alt.q: Which combining form would Dr. Boardman use to refer to Martin's heart?
alt.ex: cardi/o is the combining form for heart.

alt.q: Martin asks what 'cardio' in cardiomyopathy refers to. The best plain-language answer is
alt.ex: cardi/o means heart.

sc.title: Cardiomyopathy terminology
sc.text: Alvin Boardman is a Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine (DO) working in a primary care clinic. Dr. Boardman is telling a patient, Martin, that recent tests show a new diagnosis of a cardiomyopathy, and Martin will require more testing to determine the most appropriate treatment plan.

items.q: The combining form "my/o" refers to which body part?
items.ex: my/o means muscle, so cardiomyopathy involves the heart muscle.

alt.q: In 'cardiomyopathy,' the 'my/o' part tells Martin that the disease affects the heart's
alt.ex: my/o means muscle, so cardiomyopathy is a disease of the heart muscle.

alt.q: Which combining form has the same meaning as my/o?
alt.ex: Both my/o and muscul/o mean muscle.

sc.title: Cardiomyopathy terminology
sc.text: Alvin Boardman is a Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine (DO) working in a primary care clinic. Dr. Boardman is telling a patient, Martin, that recent tests show a new diagnosis of a cardiomyopathy, and Martin will require more testing to determine the most appropriate treatment plan.

items.q: During the office visit, Dr. Boardman notes that Martin is experiencing bradycardia. Based on the meaning of the prefix "brady-" and the word root "cardi," what does bradycardia mean?
items.ex: brady- means slow and cardi means heart, so bradycardia is a slow heart rate.
w: -cardia refers to the heart, not breathing.
Fast breathing would use tachy- with -pnea.

alt.q: Martin's chart shows bradycardia. Which pulse reading fits this finding?
alt.ex: Bradycardia means a slow heart rate, so a rate below the normal adult range, like 48, fits.

alt.q: The prefix brady- in Martin's diagnosis of bradycardia means
alt.ex: brady- means slow, so bradycardia is a slow heart rate.

sc.title: Cardiomyopathy terminology
sc.text: Alvin Boardman is a Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine (DO) working in a primary care clinic. Dr. Boardman is telling a patient, Martin, that recent tests show a new diagnosis of a cardiomyopathy, and Martin will require more testing to determine the most appropriate treatment plan.

items.q: Dr. Boardman explains that cardiomyopathy can influence blood pressure, causing it to be elevated. Based on your knowledge of prefixes, which of the following terms means high blood pressure?
items.ex: hyper- means above or excessive, so hypertension is high blood pressure.
w: anti- means against; not a real term.
hypo- means under, so this is low blood pressure.
poly- means many; not a real term.

alt.q: If Martin's blood pressure dropped too low instead, which term would describe it?
alt.ex: hypo- means less than or under, so hypotension is low blood pressure.

alt.q: Which prefix tells Dr. Boardman that a term means 'above normal or excessive'?
alt.ex: hyper- means above or excessive, as in hypertension (high blood pressure).

sc.title: Cardiomyopathy terminology
sc.text: Alvin Boardman is a Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine (DO) working in a primary care clinic. Dr. Boardman is telling a patient, Martin, that recent tests show a new diagnosis of a cardiomyopathy, and Martin will require more testing to determine the most appropriate treatment plan.

items.q: The suffix "-pathy" means
items.ex: -pathy means disease, so cardiomyopathy is disease of the heart muscle.

alt.q: Martin's diagnosis, cardiomyopathy, ends in -pathy. The term therefore names a heart muscle
alt.ex: -pathy means disease, so cardiomyopathy is disease of the heart muscle.

alt.q: Which term means disease of the brain?
alt.ex: Encephalopathy combines encephal/o (brain) with -pathy (disease).

items.q: The ilium is the
items.ex: The ilium (with an i) is part of the hip bone; the ileum (with an e) is part of the small intestine.
w: That's the ileum, spelled with an e.
The lung lining is the pleura.
The smallest ear bone is the stapes.

alt.q: Which spelling names part of the small intestine rather than the hip bone?
alt.ex: Ileum (e) is part of the small intestine; ilium (i) is part of the hip bone.
w: A bowel blockage, not a body part.

alt.q: A chart note mentions a fracture of the ilium. Which body area was injured?
alt.ex: The ilium is part of the hip bone, so a fracture there is a hip injury.

items.q: The suffix -ism in the medical term hypothyroidism means
items.ex: -ism means condition, so hypothyroidism is a condition of lower than normal thyroid hormone.

alt.q: Hypothyroidism means a ___ created by less than normal levels of thyroid hormone.
alt.ex: -ism means condition, so hypothyroidism is a condition of low thyroid hormone.

alt.q: Which suffix means 'condition'?
alt.ex: -ism means condition, as in hypothyroidism.

items.q: If the term ends in ex or ix, the plural is usually formed by changing the ex or ix to
items.ex: Terms ending in ex or ix usually form the plural by changing ex or ix to ices (appendix → appendices).
w: -ges replaces x in terms ending in nx.

alt.q: What is the plural of appendix?
alt.ex: Terms ending in ix change ix to ices, so appendix becomes appendices.

alt.q: Following the ex/ix plural rule, the plural of 'index' is
alt.ex: Change ex to ices: index becomes indices.
w: -e is added to words ending in a.

items.q: The abbreviation b.i.d. means ____ times a day.
items.ex: b.i.d. (bid) means twice a day.
w: Once a day was q.d., now written as 'daily.'
Three times a day is t.i.d.
Four times a day is q.i.d.

alt.q: Which abbreviation means twice a day?
alt.ex: b.i.d. (bid) means twice a day.

alt.q: A medication ordered b.i.d. for 5 days results in how many total doses?
alt.ex: b.i.d. means twice a day, so 2 doses × 5 days = 10 doses.

items.q: Hemiplegia is best described as _____
items.a: Paralysis on one side of the body
items.ex: hemi- means half and -plegia means paralysis, so hemiplegia is paralysis of one side of the body.
w: Numbness on both sides of the body
-plegia is paralysis, not numbness; hemi- is half.
Not one side; quadriplegia is all four limbs.

alt.q: After a stroke, a patient cannot move the right arm and right leg. Which term fits?
alt.ex: hemi- (half) + -plegia (paralysis) = paralysis of one side of the body.

alt.q: In 'hemiplegia,' what do the two word parts mean?
alt.ex: hemi- means half and -plegia means paralysis.
w: bi- means two; hemi- means half.

items.q: Which of the following combining forms means rib?
items.ex: cost/o is the combining form for rib.

alt.q: Intercostal means between the
alt.ex: inter- (between) + cost/o (rib) = between the ribs.

alt.q: Which part of the body does cost/o refer to?
alt.ex: cost/o is the combining form for rib.

items.q: Which of the following terms means the study of the heart?
items.ex: -logy means study of, so cardiology is the study of the heart.
w: Carditis is inflammation of the heart.
Cardiomyopathy is disease of the heart muscle.

alt.q: Which suffix would you add to cardi/o to name the study of the heart?
alt.ex: -logy means study of: cardi/o + -logy = cardiology.

alt.q: Following the same pattern as cardiology, what does 'neurology' mean?
alt.ex: neur/o (nerve) + -logy (study of) = the study of the nerves.

items.q: The combining form derm/o refers to ____
items.ex: derm/o (and dermat/o) means skin.
w: enter/o is small intestine; col/o is large intestine.

alt.q: A dermatologist specializes in conditions of the
alt.ex: dermat/o means skin, so a dermatologist treats skin conditions.

alt.q: Which combining form has the same meaning as derm/o?
alt.ex: derm/o and dermat/o both mean skin.

items.q: The combining forms adip/o, lip/o, and steat/o all mean which of the following?
items.ex: adip/o, lip/o, and steat/o are three combining forms that all mean fat.

alt.q: Which combining form does NOT mean fat?
alt.ex: oste/o means bone; adip/o, lip/o, and steat/o all mean fat.

alt.q: A lipoma is a tumor made up of which tissue?
alt.ex: lip/o (fat) + -oma (tumor) = a fatty tumor.

items.q: The combining form that means liver is ____
items.ex: hepat/o is the combining form for liver.

alt.q: Hepatomegaly refers to enlargement of the
alt.ex: hepat/o means liver and -megaly means enlargement.

alt.q: The combining form hepat/o refers to which organ?
alt.ex: hepat/o is the combining form for liver.

items.q: The medical term that means an examination of the abdomen with a scope is
items.ex: lapar/o means abdominal wall and -scopy means examination using a scope, so laparoscopy examines the abdomen with a scope.
w: A general scope exam inside the body, not specific to the abdomen.
This examines the esophagus, stomach, and duodenum.

alt.q: Which suffix in 'laparoscopy' indicates an examination using a scope?
alt.ex: -scopy means examination using a scope; -scope is the instrument.

alt.q: lapar/o + -scopy combines to mean an examination of the
alt.ex: lapar/o means abdominal wall, so laparoscopy is a scope exam of the abdomen.

items.q: What does carditis mean?
items.ex: cardi (heart) + -itis (inflammation) = carditis, inflammation of the heart.
w: Surgery terms use endings like -otomy or -ectomy.
The study of the heart is cardiology.

alt.q: Which term means inflammation of the stomach?
alt.ex: -itis means inflammation, as in carditis and gastritis.

alt.q: A patient diagnosed with carditis has
alt.ex: cardi (heart) + -itis (inflammation) = carditis.
w: a rupture of the heart wall

items.q: A gastrectomy is the removal of all or part of the stomach.
items.ex: -ectomy means surgical removal, so gastrectomy is removal of part or all of the stomach.
items.ww: -ectomy means surgical removal; gastr means stomach.

alt.q: Appendectomy and gastrectomy share a suffix that means surgical removal.
alt.ex: -ectomy means surgical removal of the part named by the root.

alt.q: A gastrectomy is a surgical incision into the stomach in which no tissue is removed.
alt.ex: An incision is -otomy; a gastrectomy removes all or part of the stomach.

items.q: Venostasis is the stoppage of blood in an extremity.
items.ex: -stasis means stoppage and ven/o means vein. Table 5–4 defines venostasis as 'stoppage of blood in a vein,' not in an extremity.
items.ww: The text says 'in a vein,' not 'in an extremity.'

alt.q: The suffix -stasis in venostasis means stoppage or controlling.
alt.ex: -stasis means stoppage, controlling, or standing.

alt.q: Venostasis means the rapid flow of blood through a vein.
alt.ex: -stasis means stoppage, so venostasis is the stopping, not rapid flow, of blood in a vein.

items.q: Excretion of large amounts of urine is
items.ex: poly- means many or much, so polyuria is excretion of large amounts of urine.
w: Just a word part for urine, not a full term.
Anuria is absence of urine formation.

alt.q: A patient with polyuria would most likely report
alt.ex: poly- means many or much, so polyuria is excretion of large amounts of urine.

alt.q: In 'polyuria,' the prefix poly- means
alt.ex: poly- means many or much.

items.q: Which of the following is a suffix that means enlarged?
items.ex: -megaly means enlargement, as in cardiomegaly (enlarged heart).

alt.q: Hepatomegaly means the liver is
alt.ex: -megaly means enlargement.

alt.q: Which term describes an enlarged heart?
alt.ex: cardi/o + -megaly = cardiomegaly, an enlarged heart.

items.q: The term neuritis means _______.
items.ex: neur (nerve) + -itis (inflammation) = neuritis, inflammation of the nerve.

alt.q: Which suffix in 'neuritis' signals inflammation?
alt.ex: -itis means inflammation of.

alt.q: A patient has inflammation of a nerve. Which term names this?
alt.ex: neur (nerve) + -itis (inflammation) = neuritis.

items.q: The study of medical terminology includes all the following, EXCEPT which of the following?
items.a: Learning to perform a physical exam
items.ex: Medical terminology covers terms, abbreviations, and symbols; performing a physical exam is a clinical skill.
w: Symbols are part of medical terminology.
Terms are the core of it.

alt.q: Which skill falls OUTSIDE the study of medical terminology?
alt.ex: Taking blood pressure is a clinical skill; terminology covers terms, abbreviations, and symbols.
w: Learning medical symbols such as Δ
Decoding word roots and their suffixes

alt.q: A student studying medical terminology should expect to learn which set of items?
alt.ex: Medical terminology includes terms plus their abbreviations and symbols.
w: Exams and surgeries are clinical skills.
Dosages and labs are other skills.

items.q: The prefix auto- means against.
items.ex: auto- means self (as in autoimmune); anti- is the prefix that means against.
items.ww: auto- = self; anti- = against.

alt.q: The prefix anti- means against, as in antibiotic.
alt.ex: anti- means against; an antibiotic inhibits or destroys microorganisms.

alt.q: An autoimmune response is an immune reaction against outside germs.
alt.ex: auto- means self, so autoimmune is an immune response to one's own body.

items.q: The Institute for Safe Medication Practices recommends not using abbreviations for drugs.
items.ex: The Institute for Safe Medication Practices recommends that drug names not be abbreviated because abbreviations can cause errors.
items.ww: ISMP recommends against abbreviating drug names.

alt.q: The Institute for Safe Medication Practices encourages abbreviating long drug names to save time.
alt.ex: ISMP recommends that drug names not be abbreviated.
alt.ww: ISMP says don't abbreviate drug names.

alt.q: ISMP keeps a list of error-prone abbreviations and symbols that it recommends never using.
alt.ex: The Institute created this list after reported errors.
alt.ww: The text describes this ISMP list.

items.q: The do-not-use list contains suggestions for medical terms that should be avoided when speaking with patients.
items.ex: The do-not-use list names error-prone abbreviations (such as U, IU, q.d., and q.o.d.) that must not be used in documentation, not words to avoid with patients.
items.ww: It lists error-prone abbreviations, not words to avoid with patients.

alt.q: The Joint Commission requires accredited organizations to have a do-not-use list of abbreviations.
alt.ex: Certain abbreviations must appear on an accredited organization's do-not-use list.

alt.q: The do-not-use list contains medical words that are too complex to explain to patients.
alt.ex: It contains error-prone abbreviations such as U, IU, q.d., and q.o.d.
alt.ww: It lists abbreviations, not complex words.

items.q: Which of the following abbreviations should not be used?
items.ex: QD (every day) is on the do-not-use list because it can be misread as QID; write 'daily.'
w: TID (three times a day) is not on the do-not-use list.
PO (by mouth) is an approved abbreviation.
BID (twice a day) is not on the do-not-use list.

alt.q: Instead of writing 'QD' on an order, the text says to write
alt.ex: QD is on the do-not-use list; write 'daily' instead.
w: Four times a day; a different order.

alt.q: Why does the do-not-use list ban 'QD'?
alt.a: It may be misread as QID
alt.ex: The period after q or the tail of the Q can look like an 'I,' turning daily into four times a day.
w: It may be misread as a zero
It may be misread as IV
It may be misread as PO

items.q: An otoscope is an instrument used to examine the eye.
items.ex: An otoscope is an instrument used to examine the ear (ot/o = ear).
items.ww: ot/o means ear; ophthalm/o means eye.

alt.q: The combining form ot/o in otoscope refers to the ear.
alt.ex: ot/o means ear, and -scope is the instrument used to view.

alt.q: The suffix -scope in otoscope means the examination itself rather than the instrument.
alt.ex: -scope is the instrument used to view; -scopy is the examination.

items.q: Only approved abbreviations can be used in medical documentation.
items.ex: Each facility has an approved list, and using abbreviations not on it is against state and federal regulatory guidelines.
items.ww: Only abbreviations on the facility's approved list may be used.

alt.q: Staff may use their own personal abbreviations in charts as long as coworkers understand them.
alt.ex: Never substitute personal versions; use only the approved list.

alt.q: A facility can be cited if unapproved abbreviations are found during an accreditation survey.
alt.ex: Using abbreviations not on the approved list breaks regulatory guidelines.
alt.ww: The text says the facility can be cited.

items.q: When choosing a medical dictionary, it is important to check the coverage of terms.
items.ex: The text says to check that a dictionary covers the terms used in your occupational area.
items.ww: Coverage of terms is an important feature.

alt.q: All medical dictionaries cover the same terms, so coverage doesn't matter when choosing one.
alt.ex: Some dictionaries are more inclusive; check coverage in your specialty.

alt.q: Pronunciation hints and clear definitions are useful features in a medical dictionary.
alt.ex: Both are listed features to look for.

items.q: What is the plural of diverticulum?
items.ex: Terms ending in um change um to a, so diverticulum becomes diverticula.
w: -ae is for words ending in a.
Diverticulosis is a condition, not a plural.

alt.q: Which term follows the same plural rule as diverticulum?
alt.ex: Terms ending in um change um to a: diverticulum → diverticula, ovum → ova.

alt.q: A colonoscopy finds more than one diverticulum. The report should use the term
alt.ex: Change um to a: one diverticulum, two diverticula.

items.q: Palpation is pounding of the heart.
items.ex: Palpation is feeling a body part with the hands to examine it; palpitations is pounding of the heart.
items.ww: That's palpitations, not palpation.

alt.q: Palpitations is the term for a pounding of the heart.
alt.ex: Palpitations means pounding of the heart; palpation is examining by touch.
alt.ww: The text defines palpitations this way.

alt.q: Palpitations means examining a body part by feeling it with the hands.
alt.ex: That is palpation; palpitations is pounding of the heart.

items.q: What does the suffix -emia mean?
items.ex: -emia means blood or blood condition, as in bacteremia.

alt.q: Bacteremia means
alt.ex: -emia means blood or blood condition.

alt.q: Which suffix would complete a term meaning a blood condition?
alt.ex: -emia means blood or a blood condition.

items.q: Which of the following is an example of a combining form?
items.ex: A combining form is a word root plus a combining vowel, shown with a slash: gastr/o.
w: A word root without the combining vowel.

alt.q: A word root plus a combining vowel is a combining form. Which item fits?
alt.ex: oste/o is the root oste plus the combining vowel o.

alt.q: What makes cardi/o a combining form rather than just a word root?
alt.a: It adds the vowel o to the root
alt.ex: A combining form is a word root plus a combining vowel, usually o.
w: It always goes at the start of a term
It always goes at the end of a term
It is named after a discovering doctor

items.q: If a patient has an order for NPO and their breakfast tray arrives, what is the most appropriate action?
items.a: Do not take the breakfast tray to the patient's room.
items.ex: NPO means nothing by mouth, so the breakfast tray should not go to the patient.
w: Take the breakfast tray to the patient's room.
NPO means nothing by mouth; don't deliver food.
The order is clear; just hold the tray.
Remove the items that are not liquid, and then take it to the patient's room.

alt.q: A patient on NPO asks for a glass of water. What is the correct response?
alt.a: Hold the water and explain the order
alt.ex: NPO means nothing by mouth, including water.
w: Give a small sip since it's only water
Give water but hold all solid foods
Let the patient get water on their own

alt.q: What does NPO mean?
alt.ex: NPO means nothing by mouth.

items.q: The combining form cephal/o means
items.ex: cephal/o means head.

alt.q: Cephalalgia means pain in the
alt.ex: cephal/o (head) + -algia (pain) = head pain.

alt.q: Which combining form refers to the head?
alt.ex: cephal/o means head; encephal/o means brain.

items.q: Which of the following is an example of a whole number?
items.ex: Whole numbers are the counting numbers (1, 2, 3...) and contain no fractions or decimals, so 7 is a whole number.

alt.q: Which number is NOT a whole number?
alt.ex: 30.5 contains a decimal; whole numbers have no fractions or decimals.

alt.q: Which statement describes whole numbers?
alt.a: Counting numbers with no fraction or decimal
alt.ex: Whole numbers are the numbers we count with (1, 2, 3...) and contain no fractions or decimals.
w: Numbers that must always contain a decimal point
Parts of a whole written over a denominator
Numbers expressed as a part of one hundred

items.q: What is the first step in overcoming math anxiety?
items.ex: The first step to overcoming math anxiety is to recognize that it exists and be willing to do something about it.
w: Not the first step the text gives.
Ignoring it doesn't help; recognize it first.
A helpful later step, not the first.

alt.q: Genevieve fears an upcoming math course. According to the text, what should Genevieve do first?
alt.a: Identify that math anxiety is present
alt.ex: The first step to overcoming math anxiety is recognizing that it exists.
w: Delay the course until the fear fades
Memorize every formula ahead of time
Accept that math ability is genetic

alt.q: A student says, 'I just freeze up whenever I see numbers.' What is the best first move?
alt.a: Admit the anxiety and choose to act
alt.ex: The first step is to recognize the anxiety exists and be willing to do something about it.
w: Skip math classes until it goes away
Wait to learn a secret math trick
There are no secrets to be handed out.
Blame a poor memory and give up
A false belief; understanding beats memory.

items.q: Which of the following is not a calculation task required by health care professionals?
items.a: Finding the square root of a number
items.ex: The text lists dosages, height and weight, intake and output, billing, lab tests, solutions, claims, and payments, but not square roots.
w: Listed as a health care math task.
Listed as a health care math task.
Listed as a health care math task.

alt.q: Which task listed in the text requires math skills in health care?
alt.ex: Mixing solutions is one of the math applications listed for health care.

alt.q: Which task is NOT one of the math applications the text lists for health care?
alt.ex: The text lists practical tasks like claims, lab tests, and billing, not advanced math like calculus.

items.q: Which of the following breaks the rule to never use a trailing zero?
items.ex: A trailing zero is a zero after the decimal point that follows a whole number, as in 6.0; write 6 instead.
w: Odd extra zero in front, but not a trailing zero.

alt.q: A provider wants a 3-milligram dose. Which way of writing it follows the decimal rules?
alt.ex: Never use a trailing zero; write 3 mg, not 3.0 mg.
w: Trailing zero; could be read as 30 mg.

alt.q: Why should a dose never be written as 5.0 mg?
alt.a: It could be misread as 50 mg
alt.ex: If the decimal point is missed, 5.0 mg looks like 50 mg, a tenfold overdose.
w: It could be misread as 0.5 mg
A missed decimal makes it larger, not smaller.
It could be misread as 5 grams
It is less exact than writing 5
Not the risk; it's a misreading risk.

items.q: How can errors be made when utilizing the traditional time system?
items.a: Not noting a.m. or p.m. in documentation
items.ex: If a.m. or p.m. is omitted or misread in the traditional system, a 12-hour error results.
w: Four digits are used in military time, which prevents errors.
Not itself the source of the error.

alt.q: A medication given at 7:00 is charted without a.m. or p.m. How large an error could result?
alt.ex: Omitting or misreading a.m./p.m. creates a 12-hour error.
w: That's a full day; the shift is 12 hours.

alt.q: Why is military time often used in health care?
alt.ex: The 24-hour clock prevents the 12-hour errors caused by missing or misread a.m. and p.m.
w: It uses fewer digits per time
It is required for all billing

items.q: On which whole unit would a patient's height be measured using the metric system?
items.ex: The meter is the metric whole (base) unit for distance and length, so height is measured with it.
w: Kilo is a prefix meaning 1,000 times, not a unit.
The liter measures capacity and volume.
The yard is a household unit.

alt.q: A patient's height is recorded in centimeters. Which metric base unit is being modified?
alt.ex: Centi- modifies the meter, the metric base unit for distance and length.

alt.q: Which metric unit would NOT be used to record a patient's height?
alt.ex: Liters measure capacity and volume; height uses the meter and its prefixed units.

items.q: Which of the following best describes math anxiety?
items.ex: The text says math anxiety is also called math avoidance or math phobia.
w: A possible effect, not what the condition is.
A possible result, not the condition.

alt.q: Which is a sign of math anxiety described in the text?
alt.ex: People with math anxiety may fear mistakes, freeze up and go blank, or fear being judged.

alt.q: Which term is another name for math anxiety?
alt.ex: The text says math anxiety is also called math avoidance or math phobia.
w: A learning disability, not the text's term.
Not a term the text uses.
Not a term the text uses.

items.q: A health care professional must strive for a ______ level of accuracy when administering medications.
items.ex: Medication errors can harm or even kill patients, so health care professionals must strive for 100% accuracy.

alt.q: A coworker says getting 98% of doses right is good enough. What does the text say?
alt.ex: Medication errors can harm or kill patients, so professionals must strive for 100% accuracy.

alt.q: What is the most serious potential result of a math error when giving medication?
alt.a: Harm or death of the patient
alt.ex: A wrong dosage can harm or even cause the death of a patient.
w: A lower score on a job review

items.q: How can health care providers minimize the risk of computer-generated medication errors?
items.ex: Computerized orders still contain misread characters (l/1, O/0, Z/2), so entries should be checked by hand rather than trusted blindly.
w: Avoid using computers for medication orders.
Computer entry overcomes most handwriting errors; avoiding it isn't the fix.
Rely solely on the computer system.

alt.q: Computerized order entry has reduced handwriting errors. Which statement is accurate?
alt.a: It still does not prevent all errors
alt.ex: Even typed orders can be misread, such as l for 1 or O for 0.
w: It prevents every possible med error
Typed orders can still be misread.
It removes any need to verify doses

alt.q: The ISMP reports that which character mix-ups cause over half of misidentification errors?
alt.ex: l/1, O/0, Z/2, plus 1 mistaken for 7 account for over 50% of these errors.
w: Not the pairs the text names.
Not the pairs the text names.

items.q: What is 1,379 rounded to the nearest thousand?
items.ex: The hundreds digit of 1,379 is 3 (less than 5), so it rounds down to 1,000.
w: That's rounding to the nearest hundred.
That's rounding to the nearest ten.

alt.q: What is 2,681 rounded to the nearest thousand?
alt.ex: The hundreds digit is 6 (5 or above), so 2,681 rounds up to 3,000.
w: The 6 in the hundreds place means round up.

alt.q: What is 5,449 rounded to the nearest thousand?
alt.ex: The hundreds digit is 4 (less than 5), so 5,449 rounds down to 5,000.
w: The 4 in the hundreds place means round down.

items.q: How many milliliters (mL) is in two ounces?
items.ex: 1 oz = 30 mL, so 2 oz × 30 = 60 mL.

alt.q: How many milliliters are in 5 ounces?
alt.ex: 1 oz = 30 mL, so 5 oz × 30 = 150 mL.

alt.q: A patient drinks 90 mL of juice. How many ounces is that?
alt.ex: 90 mL ÷ 30 mL per ounce = 3 oz.

sc.title: Oliver - medical math
sc.text: Oliver is a nursing student at the local university. This semester, Oliver is taking a medical math class that has been particularly challenging. Oliver is getting ready to take the midterm, which is known to be extremely difficult for this class. Oliver tells their friend Kate, “I don’t even understand the point of all this math! I am training to be a nurse, not a pharmacist!”

sc.title: Quinn - fractured forearm
sc.text:
Twelve-year-old Quinn was playing basketball with some friends when they fell and landed on their outstretched arm, causing a twisting motion followed by sudden pain for Quinn. Quinn’s parents rush Quinn to the emergency department, where they meet with Nurse Practitioner Kayla to assess Quinn's injury.

Kayla carefully examines Quinn's arm and believes the arm to be broken. Kayla orders X-rays to determine the extent of the injury. After reviewing the results, Kayla explains to Quinn's parents that Quinn has a fractured radius, one of the two bones in the forearm. Kayla reassures them

that Quinn will receive the necessary treatment to promote healing and restore full function to the arm.

As Quinn's parents express concern about the recovery process, Kayla provides them with information about treatment and care. Quinn will need to wear a plaster-based cast on the arm to keep the bones set during the healing process and keep Quinn from causing more damage to the arm during the healing process. Kayla is also concerned with managing Quinn’s pain and explains the importance of taking the prescribed medication as needed, elevating the arm, and using cold compresses to reduce swelling.

items.q: How does understanding anatomy and physiology benefit Nurse Practitioner Kayla in assessing and treating Quinn's fractured arm?
items.a: Knowledge of anatomy and physiology allows Kayla to recognize the signs and symptoms of Quinn's injury, facilitating an accurate diagnosis and treatment plan.
items.ex: Knowing normal structure and function lets Kayla recognize abnormal signs and symptoms, leading to an accurate diagnosis and treatment plan.
w: Understanding anatomy and physiology helps Kayla empathize with Quinn's pain and discomfort, leading to better communication with Quinn's parents.
Empathy matters, but it is not the main benefit of A&P knowledge.
Understanding anatomy and physiology enables Kayla to perform surgery to repair Quinn's fractured arm more effectively.
Kayla is not doing surgery; not the benefit described.
Knowledge of anatomy and physiology enables Kayla to prescribe medication to Quinn without considering potential side effects.

alt.q: Why does Kayla's knowledge of normal arm structure and function matter in Quinn's care?
alt.ex: Understanding the normal body gives a base for recognizing abnormal conditions.
w: It lets Kayla skip ordering the X-rays
It replaces taking the patient history
It guarantees a faster healing time

alt.q: Which action by Kayla best shows anatomy and physiology knowledge in use?
alt.a: Linking Quinn's pain to a radius fracture
alt.ex: Connecting symptoms to a specific bone injury applies A&P knowledge.
w: Calming Quinn's parents in the waiting room
Scheduling a follow-up visit for next month
Completing the insurance paperwork for Quinn
