w: Tell the patient to wait until stronger
Order more blood tests and X-rays

items.q: Which of the following terms refers to actions such as eating, toileting, dressing, and cleaning?
items.ex: Activities of daily living are regular actions done to meet physical needs, such as eating, toileting, dressing, and cleaning.
w: An H&P is the provider's history and exam.
A general survey is an overall look at the patient.
Vital signs are TPR, oxygen saturation, and B/P.

alt.q: Which of these is an activity of daily living?
alt.ex: The textbook lists paying bills along with bathing, eating, dressing, and laundry as ADLs.

alt.q: A patient can no longer turn in bed or walk without help. What does this describe?
alt.a: Trouble with activities of daily living
alt.ex: Turning in bed and ambulating are ADLs, so this patient has trouble with ADLs.
w: Abnormal vital signs found on admission day
Vital signs are temperature, pulse, etc.
A problem found in the general survey
The general survey is a broader first look.
A change in their psychosocial status
Psychosocial covers emotion and mental status.

items.q: Which term describes behaviors such as wincing, limping, and restlessness when observed by a health care professional?
items.ex: Limping, favoring an area, moaning, restlessness, and wincing are nonverbal cues that may indicate pain.
w: Too general; these are specifically pain cues.
Psychosocial covers emotions and mental status.
Verbal cues are things the patient says.

alt.q: Which of these is a nonverbal cue that a patient may be in pain?
alt.a: Favoring one area of the body
alt.ex: The textbook lists favoring an area, limping, moaning, restlessness, and wincing.
w: That is a verbal pain rating.
Saying out loud that their back hurts

alt.q: A patient says they are fine but keeps wincing when they move. What should the health care professional note?
alt.a: A nonverbal sign of possible pain
alt.ex: Wincing is a nonverbal cue that can indicate pain even if the patient denies it.
w: Wincing is a possible pain cue.
A verbal sign that the pain is gone
A sign of an abnormal pulse rate

items.q: Which of the following terms refers to difficulty breathing?
items.ex: Dyspnea means difficulty breathing.
w: Cyanosis is bluish discoloration of skin or nail beds.
Orthopnea is breathing easier when sitting up.

alt.q: A patient becomes short of breath when climbing stairs. Which term describes this?
alt.ex: Dyspnea is difficulty breathing; on exertion means with activity.
w: Bradypnea is a slow breathing rate.

alt.q: What does the term orthopnea describe?
alt.ex: Orthopnea is when a patient breathes easier in a sitting position.
w: A bluish color to the skin

items.q: Which of the following is the purpose of performing a general survey of the patient?
items.a: To get overall look at the patient as a whole
items.ex: A general survey gives an overall impression of the patient as a whole before focusing on systems.
w: Vital signs are only one part of the survey.
Pain assessment is a separate evaluation.
To assess each of the body systems
Reviewing each system is the head-to-toe assessment.

alt.q: What problem is the general survey meant to prevent?
alt.a: Forgetting to see the patient as a whole
alt.ex: Studying systems separately can make staff forget to look at the whole patient.
w: Forgetting to take the patient's pulse
The survey isn't only about pulse.
Charting the wrong date on the patient's H&P
Using the wrong pain scale for age
That is part of pain evaluation.

alt.q: Which question is part of a general survey?
alt.a: Does the patient look strong or ill?
alt.ex: The general survey asks for the overall impression, such as healthy versus weak and ill.
w: What is the patient's insurance plan?
How many siblings does the patient have?
That is family history in the H&P.
Which pharmacy does the patient use?

items.q: Which of the following terms refers to listening to body sounds using a stethoscope?
items.ex: Auscultation is listening to sounds inside the body with a stethoscope, such as lung, heart, and bowel sounds.
w: Percussion is lightly tapping with the fingertips.
Palpation is feeling with the hands and fingers.
Inspection uses vision, hearing, and smell.

alt.q: Listening to a patient's bowel sounds with a stethoscope is an example of what?
alt.ex: Auscultation is listening inside the body with a stethoscope, including bowel sounds.
w: That is feeling with the hands.
That is tapping with the fingertips.
That is observing with the senses.

alt.q: Which technique uses the hands and fingers to detect abnormalities in internal organs?
alt.ex: Palpation uses the hands and fingers on the outside of the body to detect abnormalities.
w: That is listening with a stethoscope.
That is lightly tapping the body.

items.q: Which route for taking a temperature is the least accurate?
items.ex: The textbook calls the axillary route the least accurate method.
w: Oral is a standard, accurate route.
Rectal is a standard route that runs a degree higher.

alt.q: When is the axillary route usually used?
alt.a: When oral isn't right and no ear thermometer
alt.ex: The axillary route is used when the oral route isn't appropriate and an aural thermometer isn't available.
w: For every adult patient at each office visit
It is the least accurate, so not routine.
Whenever a patient has a high fever
Fever doesn't call for this route.
Only for patients right after eating

alt.q: How does a normal axillary temperature compare to an oral temperature?
alt.ex: The axillary route normally runs about one degree lower than the oral route.
w: Oral and aural are the same.
Axillary runs lower than oral, not higher.

items.q: Which statement below describes the definition of high blood pressure for adults (19 years of age or older)?
items.a: Blood pressure reading guidelines are the same for all adults.
items.ex: Updated guidelines removed age differences, so the same blood pressure categories apply to all adults.
w: Blood pressure reading guidelines vary with age for adults.
Guidelines no longer vary by age.
Blood pressure reading guidelines decrease with age.
Blood pressure reading guidelines increase with age.
Older adults no longer get higher thresholds.

alt.q: What blood pressure is now generally defined as high blood pressure in adults?
alt.ex: High blood pressure is now 130 or higher for the top number or 80 or higher for the bottom.

alt.q: A 70-year-old and a 30-year-old both have readings of 134/84. How are they classified?
alt.ex: The same categories apply to all adults, and 130–139 / 80–89 is stage 1.
w: Both readings are in the normal range

items.q: Which method can be used to obtain a height measurement when an adult patient cannot stand?
items.a: Take the measurement when the patient is lying down.
items.ex: If a patient can't stand, height is measured lying flat by marking the top of the head and the heels.
w: Ask several staff to help the patient to stand up.
Forcing a patient to stand is unsafe.
Skip the measurement as adult heights do not change.
Adult height should be measured yearly.

alt.q: How is height measured for a patient who must stay in bed?
alt.a: Mark head and heels, measure between
alt.ex: Place the patient flat and straight, mark the top of the head and bottom of the heels, and measure.
w: Use the height from their driver's license
Measure from the shoulders to the feet
Measure from the top of the head.
Copy the height from last year's chart

alt.q: Besides adults who can't stand, who else is measured lying down?
alt.a: Infants and children who can't stand
alt.ex: The lying-down method is also used for infants and children unable to stand.
w: All adults over age 65 at every visit
Those who can stand are measured standing.
Any patient who has a fever today

items.q: Which of the following is used to determine if the patient is at a healthy weight?
items.ex: Many facilities use BMI to determine if a patient is at a healthy weight.
w: An ADL evaluation looks at daily activities.
Vital signs don't measure healthy weight.
Psychosocial observation looks at emotions and mental status.

alt.q: What is a known limitation of BMI?
alt.a: It may be off for very muscular people
alt.ex: BMI can be inaccurate if a person is very muscular or has lost a lot of muscle mass.
w: It can only be used on children
It is used for adults too.
It requires a blood test to calculate it

alt.q: A patient's weight is 70 kg and height is 1.75 m. What is the BMI, to one decimal?
alt.ex: BMI = weight (kg) divided by height (m) squared: 70 / (1.75 × 1.75) = 22.9.

items.q: Which information is used to determine how the patient is progressing in relation to how they were at a particular point in time?
items.ex: The baseline from the H&P is used to see how the patient is progressing compared with an earlier point in time.
w: Normal is a general range, not this patient's starting point.
Too general; physical data alone isn't the baseline.

alt.q: Where does a patient's baseline information first come from?
alt.ex: The information obtained during the H&P is considered the baseline.

alt.q: Why should health care professionals review the H&P at later visits?
alt.a: To compare changes to the baseline
alt.ex: Reviewing the H&P increases understanding of how the patient's condition has changed.
w: To check the provider's signature line
Not the reason for reviewing it.
To copy old vital signs forward
Never assume readings are the same.

items.q: Which of the following terms refers to the information used to detect variances from the normal collected by unlicensed personnel?
items.ex: When unlicensed health care professionals ask questions and make observations, it is called data collection.
w: Assessment is restricted to licensed professionals.
A general survey is an overall look at the patient.
An H&P is done by the provider.

alt.q: A medical assistant notices and records that a patient is limping. What is this called?
alt.ex: Observations by unlicensed staff are called data collection.
w: That term is for licensed staff.
That is listening with a stethoscope.

alt.q: How does data collection by unlicensed staff help licensed staff?
alt.a: It guides them to do more assessments
alt.ex: Data collected by unlicensed staff often guides licensed personnel to do further assessments.
w: It replaces the need for any assessment
It is used only for insurance billing
It is kept private from the provider

items.q: Which of the following measurements can indicate that medications may not be working in a patient with kidney or cardiac conditions?
items.ex: Patients with kidney or cardiac conditions are weighed to check how well their treatment is working, since fluid retention shows on the scale.
w: Temperature reflects infection, not fluid balance.

alt.q: Why is weight helpful for spotting fluid retention early?
alt.a: It shows on the scale before swelling
alt.ex: Retained fluid appears on the scale long before it is visible as edema.
w: It shows up only once swelling appears
It measures the fluid in the lungs
It is more accurate than BMI

alt.q: A patient with heart failure gained 4 pounds in two days. What might this suggest?
alt.ex: Quick weight gain in cardiac patients can mean fluid retention and that treatment may not be working.

items.q: Which system is being assessed when the health care provider observes gait and strength?
items.ex: Gait and muscle strength are observed when checking the musculoskeletal system.
w: The circulatory check covers pulses, refill, and swelling.
Gait and strength observations are listed under the musculoskeletal check.
The endocrine system has no specific listed questions.

alt.q: Which question belongs to a musculoskeletal check?
alt.a: Is there pain or stiffness with movement?
alt.ex: The musculoskeletal check asks about discomfort with movement, gait, and strength.
w: Is there any ringing in the patient's ears?
When was the patient's last bowel movement?
Is there burning when the patient urinates?

alt.q: Which observation would a health care professional make for the musculoskeletal system?
alt.a: Can the patient turn in bed alone?
alt.ex: Muscle strength is checked by asking if the patient can turn in bed without help.
w: Is the nail bed slow to turn pink?
Is the urine cloudy or clear?
Do the pupils react to light?
That is a nervous system check.

items.q: Which type of information included in a comprehensive history and physical (H&P) includes information about the patient's emotional and mental status?
items.ex: Psychosocial observations include the patient's emotional status, mental status, and appearance.
w: Physical data covers the body systems.

alt.q: Which question would be part of a psychosocial observation?
alt.a: Is the patient anxious or depressed?
alt.ex: Emotional status, such as anxiety or depression, is part of psychosocial observation.
w: That is a vital sign check.
Is the patient's skin warm or cool to touch?
Is the patient's gait normal or altered?

alt.q: A patient arrives poorly groomed and wearing shorts in freezing weather. What type of observation is this?
alt.ex: Appearance, such as dressing for the weather and grooming, is part of psychosocial status.

items.q: Which range below is the normal range for a newborn's pulse?
items.ex: Table 19–2 gives a newborn's normal pulse range as 120–160 beats per minute.
w: That is the school-age child range.

alt.q: What is the normal pulse range for an adolescent or adult, per the textbook?
alt.ex: Table 19–2 lists 60–90 for adolescents and adults, with an average of 80.

alt.q: A newborn's pulse is 140. How should this be interpreted?
alt.a: It is normal for a newborn
alt.ex: 140 is the average newborn pulse and within the 120–160 range.
w: It is too slow for a newborn
It is too fast for a newborn
It means the baby has a fever

items.q: Which of the following can only be performed by a licensed health care professional?
items.ex: The term assessment is restricted to activities done by licensed health care professionals.
w: A general survey can be done by any health care professional.
Data collection is what unlicensed staff do.

alt.q: What is the difference between assessment and data collection?
alt.a: Assessment is done only by licensed staff
alt.ex: Assessment is limited to licensed staff; unlicensed staff do data collection.
w: Data collection is done only by physicians
There is no difference in the terms
Assessment is done only by patients

alt.q: A nursing assistant asks a patient questions and notes the answers. What should this be called?
alt.ex: When unlicensed staff ask questions and observe, it is called data collection.
w: That is done by the provider.

sc.title: Priya's morning assessments
sc.text: Priya works as a Licensed Practical Nurse (LPN) in a long-term care facility. One morning, Priya is assigned to conduct routine physical assessments for several residents. Priya begins her rounds by reviewing each resident's medical history and notes any changes in their condition since the last shift. Priya performs physical assessments, including vital signs, skin integrity checks, and assessment of activities of daily living on each of the residents.

items.q: Priya is responsible for assessing residents' ability to perform activities of daily living (ADLs). Which of the following statements best describes the importance of assessing ADLs?
items.a: To understand the residents' capabilities and coordinate appropriate assistance or support
items.ex: Assessing ADLs shows what residents can do so help can be arranged when they can't perform basic ADLs.
w: To determine the residents' eligibility for admission or discharge from the facility
ADLs aren't assessed mainly for admission decisions.
To oversee the daily operations of the facility, including staffing, budgeting, and resident activities, to ensure efficient ADL management
To perform ADLs on behalf of the residents to ensure their comfort and well-being
Staff should support, not take over, what residents can do.

alt.q: Priya finds that a resident can no longer dress without help. What should happen next?
alt.a: Help is arranged to meet that need
alt.ex: When a patient is unable to perform basic ADLs, help must be arranged.
w: The resident is discharged back home
The resident must wait a week

alt.q: Which of these would Priya assess as an activity of daily living?
alt.ex: Getting out of bed is listed as an ADL.
w: That is a nervous system check.

sc.title: Priya's morning assessments
sc.text: Priya works as a Licensed Practical Nurse (LPN) in a long-term care facility. One morning, Priya is assigned to conduct routine physical assessments for several residents. Priya begins her rounds by reviewing each resident's medical history and notes any changes in their condition since the last shift. Priya performs physical assessments, including vital signs, skin integrity checks, and assessment of activities of daily living on each of the residents.

items.q: As Priya conducts routine physical assessments for several residents in the long-term care facility, Priya begins by reviewing each resident's medical history and notes any changes in their condition since the last shift. What is the primary purpose of this initial step in the assessment process?
items.a: To establish a baseline for tracking changes in residents' conditions
items.ex: Reviewing history and comparing changes gives Priya a baseline to see how each resident is progressing.
w: To gather demographic information about the residents
Demographic data isn't the reason for this step.
To identify the chief complaints reported by the residents
Chief complaints come from the patient's own report.
To document the residents' vital signs correctly
Vital signs are measured during the exam.

alt.q: Why is it more useful for Priya to compare a resident's condition to their baseline than to general norms?
alt.a: Some residents start with known problems
alt.ex: Some patients begin with problems in the H&P, so comparing changes to their baseline is more valuable.
w: General norms are rarely accurate for anyone

alt.q: A change in a resident's condition since the last shift could mean which of the following?
alt.a: The condition is getting better or worse
alt.ex: Any change may show worsening, improvement, a new problem, or a need to change treatment.
w: The last shift charted it wrong
The resident is now ready for discharge home
Changes must be noted and reported.

sc.title: Priya's morning assessments
sc.text: Priya works as a Licensed Practical Nurse (LPN) in a long-term care facility. One morning, Priya is assigned to conduct routine physical assessments for several residents. Priya begins her rounds by reviewing each resident's medical history and notes any changes in their condition since the last shift. Priya performs physical assessments, including vital signs, skin integrity checks, and assessment of activities of daily living on each of the residents.

items.q: When evaluating a resident's pain level, what is the most effective approach for Priya to use?
items.a: Asking the resident to rate their pain on a scale of 0 to 10
items.ex: Pain is subjective, so the best approach is a pain rating scale, such as asking the resident to rate pain from 0 to 10.
w: Observing the resident's posture and body movements
Posture and movement are nonverbal cues, not the best approach.
Palpating (touching) the area where the resident reports pain
Palpation isn't how pain is rated.

alt.q: A resident rates pain as 8, gets medicine, and later rates it 7. What does this suggest?
alt.a: The pain medication plan needs review
alt.ex: A small drop means the pain medication regimen needs to be reevaluated.
w: The medicine worked very well for them
A drop of 1 is not much relief.
Pain is subjective; trust the rating.

alt.q: On a 0 to 10 pain scale, what does 10 mean?
alt.a: The worst pain the patient can imagine
alt.ex: Zero is no pain and 10 is the worst pain the patient can imagine.
w: Mild pain that is easy for them to ignore
No pain at all for the patient
Not how the scale is defined.

sc.title: Priya's morning assessments
sc.text: Priya works as a Licensed Practical Nurse (LPN) in a long-term care facility. One morning, Priya is assigned to conduct routine physical assessments for several residents. Priya begins her rounds by reviewing each resident's medical history and notes any changes in their condition since the last shift. Priya performs physical assessments, including vital signs, skin integrity checks, and assessment of activities of daily living on each of the residents.

items.q: During the physical assessment, what aspect of a resident's condition should Priya primarily consider when evaluating the respiratory system?
items.a: The resident's respiratory rate and rhythm
items.ex: The respiratory check starts with the respiratory rate and rhythm.
w: The color and temperature of the resident's skin
Skin color matters, but rate and rhythm come first.
The resident's muscle strength and gait

alt.q: While counting a resident's breathing, which three things should Priya observe?
alt.ex: The three respiratory observations are rate, rhythm, and effort.
w: B/P isn't part of this count.
Rate, oxygen level, and the body weight

alt.q: Why should Priya not tell a resident that she is counting their breaths?
alt.ex: Because respiratory rate can be consciously altered, the patient shouldn't know it is being counted.
w: It is against facility privacy rules
It takes too long to explain to them

sc.title: Priya's morning assessments
sc.text: Priya works as a Licensed Practical Nurse (LPN) in a long-term care facility. One morning, Priya is assigned to conduct routine physical assessments for several residents. Priya begins her rounds by reviewing each resident's medical history and notes any changes in their condition since the last shift. Priya performs physical assessments, including vital signs, skin integrity checks, and assessment of activities of daily living on each of the residents.

items.q: What is the primary reason that Priya takes vital signs as part of the assessment of the residents?
items.a: To provide information on the residents' overall health status and detect any abnormalities
items.ex: Vital signs give important information on a patient's status, and readings outside normal ranges may signal a problem.
w: To monitor changes in the residents' emotional and mental status
Emotional and mental status are psychosocial.
To assess the residents' ability to perform activities of daily living (ADLs)
To evaluate the residents' pain level and response to pain medication
Pain is evaluated with a rating scale.

alt.q: Which of these are vital signs according to the textbook?
alt.ex: Vital signs are temperature, pulse, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, and blood pressure.
w: Height, weight, BMI, pulse rate, and pain level
Height, weight, and BMI aren't vital signs.
Pulse, pain, blood sugar, and weight
Pain and blood sugar aren't listed.
ADLs and BMI aren't vital signs.

alt.q: A resident's blood pressure was normal yesterday. What should Priya do today?
alt.a: Measure it again and record it
alt.ex: Never assume readings are the same; inaccurate data can lead to wrong decisions.
w: Never assume readings are the same.
Skip it since it was normal
It must be measured each time.
Estimate it from the pulse rate

items.q: Noting a patient's mental and emotional states are important parts of a general survey.
items.ex: A general survey considers both physical and psychological aspects, including emotional and mental status.
items.ww: Psychosocial status is part of the general survey.

alt.q: When doing a general survey, a health care professional should note the patient's emotional responses, such as anxiety or anger.
alt.ex: Emotional status is one of the psychosocial observations made during a general survey.
alt.ww: Emotional status belongs in the survey.

alt.q: A general survey looks only at the physical body, not at the patient's mental state.
alt.ex: The general survey includes both physical and psychological aspects of the patient.
alt.ww: Mental status is part of it.

items.q: If the respiratory rate is below the normal range, it is called _________ .
items.ex: A respiratory rate below normal is called bradypnea.
w: Tachypnea is a fast breathing rate.

alt.q: An adult is breathing 10 times per minute. Which term fits?
alt.ex: The adult range is 16–20, so 10 is below normal, which is bradypnea.

alt.q: Normal, even, unlabored breathing in the normal range is called what?
alt.ex: Normal breathing is called eupnea.

items.q: It is recommended that patients be weighed _______ , after they empty their bladder.
items.ex: Patients should be weighed first thing in the morning, after emptying the bladder and before they eat or drink.
w: The same time daily is needed, not any time.

alt.q: Which of these is a guideline for weighing patients?
alt.a: Use the same scale each time
alt.ex: Using the same scale each time helps make results comparable.
w: Use the same scale each time.
Leave shoes on to save time

alt.q: Why should a patient wear the same amount of clothing at each weigh-in?
alt.ex: Same clothes, same scale, and same time help make weights comparable.
w: So height is easier to read

items.q: There are certain situations in which the arm cannot be used for blood pressure readings.
items.ex: The arm can't be used after surgery on it, a mastectomy on that side, a dialysis shunt, or an IV running into it.
items.ww: Some conditions rule out using an arm.

alt.q: Blood pressure should never be taken on an arm that has a hemodialysis shunt.
alt.ex: Patients with a dialysis shunt can never have blood pressure taken on that arm.
alt.ww: A shunt rules out that arm.

alt.q: If both arms are burned, blood pressure cannot be measured at all.
alt.ex: If neither arm is available, the popliteal artery behind the knee can be used with a thigh cuff.

items.q: If a patient's blood pressure reading falls below normal, it is called ______ .
items.ex: A blood pressure reading below normal is called hypotension.

alt.q: What is orthostatic (postural) hypotension?
alt.a: A drop in B/P when standing up
alt.ex: When blood pools in the legs on standing, B/P drops quickly and the patient may feel lightheaded.
w: A rise in B/P only at the doctor
A high B/P that has no symptoms
A slow pulse when lying in bed

alt.q: Which sign would suggest that a patient's low blood pressure needs immediate attention?
alt.ex: Dizziness, fainting, blurred vision, nausea, and fatigue with low B/P may need immediate care.
w: A steady and even gait pattern

items.q: _________ is the term used to describe ringing in the ears.
items.ex: Tinnitus is ringing in the ears.
w: Otitis media is a middle ear infection.
Rhinitis is inflammation of the nose.
Acuity refers to sharpness, such as hearing acuity.

alt.q: A patient says they hear constant ringing in one ear. What should be documented?
alt.ex: Ringing in the ears is called tinnitus.

alt.q: How can a health care professional keep lip-reading from hiding a patient's hearing loss?
alt.ex: Speaking from behind or when the patient's back is turned prevents lip-reading.

items.q: Palpation is using the fingertips to lightly tap on the exterior of the body to determine the position, size, and consistency of underlying structures.
items.ex: That describes percussion; palpation uses the hands and fingers on the body to detect abnormalities in internal organs.
items.ww: That definition is percussion, not palpation.

alt.q: Percussion means lightly tapping on the body with the fingertips to find the position, size, and consistency of structures underneath.
alt.ex: This is the textbook's definition of percussion.

alt.q: Palpation means listening to sounds inside the body with a stethoscope.
alt.ex: Listening with a stethoscope is auscultation; palpation uses the hands and fingers.

items.q: A primary care provider would normally take a history and physical at which of the following times?
items.a: When seeing a patient for the first time
items.ex: The provider takes an H&P when a patient is seen for the first time or admitted to the hospital.
w: When discharging a patient from the hospital
Discharge is not when the H&P is done.
Not every visit; it is reviewed at later visits.

alt.q: Besides a first visit, when is an H&P also done?
alt.ex: An H&P is done when patients are first seen or admitted to the hospital.
w: When a patient's bill is overdue
When a patient calls the office

alt.q: In an H&P, what is the chief complaint?
alt.a: Why the patient is seeking care
alt.ex: The chief complaint is the primary problem from the patient's view.

items.q: Being able to distinguish variances from normal anatomy and physiology is an essential skill when working with patients.
items.ex: A critical function of health care professionals is telling normal from abnormal, based on knowing normal anatomy and physiology.
items.ww: This is described as a critical skill.

alt.q: To recognize an abnormal finding, a health care professional first needs a solid understanding of normal anatomy and physiology.
alt.ex: Observation skills are based on understanding normal anatomy and physiology.

alt.q: Only the provider needs to recognize variances from normal; other staff just follow orders.
alt.ex: All health care professionals who interact with patients need strong assessment skills.
alt.ww: All patient-care staff need this skill.

items.q: The rate at which a blood pressure cuff should be deflated when taking a reading is _______ .
items.a: about 2 mm Hg at a time
items.ex: The cuff should deflate evenly at about 2 mm Hg at a time.
w: about 5 mm Hg at a time
Too fast; the first beat may be missed.
about 6 mm Hg at a time
Too fast; the first beat may be missed.
about 10 mm HG at a time
Too fast; the first beat may be missed.

alt.q: What can happen if a blood pressure cuff is deflated too quickly?
alt.a: The first sound may be missed
alt.ex: If deflated too fast, the first beat may not be heard until a lower number is reached.
w: The cuff may burst on the arm
The reading will be too high

alt.q: Before taking a manual blood pressure, a health care professional finds the radial pulse stops at 120. How high should the cuff be inflated?
alt.ex: Add 30 to the point where the radial pulse stops: 120 + 30 = 150.

items.q: The provider must sign a dictated history and physical (H&P) after it is placed in the chart. It should be dated with the day the provider signs it.
items.ex: The provider must review and sign the typed H&P, but the H&P's date is the day the H&P was done, not the day it was signed.
items.ww: The H&P is dated the day it was done.

alt.q: When a dictated H&P is typed and placed in the chart, the provider must review it for accuracy and sign it.
alt.ex: The provider reviews the typed H&P for accuracy and then signs it.
alt.ww: The provider must review and sign it.

alt.q: The date on an H&P is the day the typed copy is placed in the chart.
alt.ex: The date on an H&P is the day the H&P was done.
alt.ww: It is dated the day it was done.

items.q: Kidney problems can cause a change in weight due to _____ .
items.ex: Patients with kidney conditions often have fluid balance problems, and retained fluid shows up as weight gain.
w: Body fat isn't the stated cause.
Poor use of nutrients by the body
Nutrient use isn't the stated cause.

alt.q: What is edema?
alt.a: Swelling from extra fluid in tissues
alt.ex: Edema is swelling caused by excess fluid in the body's tissues.
w: Loss of fluid from heavy sweating
Fluid in the abdominal cavity only

alt.q: What is the main goal of first aid?

Replace care given at the hospital
That is the Good Samaritan Act.

alt.q: Which group recommends that all people take a first aid and safety course?

sc.title: Darian at the car accident
sc.text: Darian is an emergency medical technician (EMT) in a rural area. One night while in the ambulance, Darian and the other EMTs on staff respond to a car accident. When they arrive, they find a three-car accident. One car has rolled down the hill on the side of the highway. The driver of the rolled-over vehicle is standing on the side of the road. The other two vehicles still have the drivers and passengers inside.

items.q: When Darian arrives at the scene, which of the following is the first step that should be followed?
items.ex: Before approaching, assess the environment to see if it is safe, such as fire, gas, or traffic hazards.
w: Obtain consent to treat the drivers and passengers.
Consent comes after the scene is safe.
Determining what happened comes after safety and consent.

alt.q: Why should Darian keep assessing the scene after arriving, not just once?
alt.a: Conditions at the scene can change
alt.ex: The situation must be monitored continuously, such as whether smoke is increasing.
w: To count how many cars there are
To pass the time until more help comes
To decide who caused the crash

alt.q: How could Darian use bystanders at the crash?
alt.ex: Bystanders can reroute traffic, keep onlookers away, look for clues, or tend to others.

sc.title: Darian at the car accident
sc.text: Darian is an emergency medical technician (EMT) in a rural area. One night while in the ambulance, Darian and the other EMTs on staff respond to a car accident. The other two vehicles still have the drivers and passengers inside.

items.q: Darian applies a splint to one of the passenger's arms. This is most likely due to signs of what condition?
items.ex: A splint immobilizes a broken bone or dislocated joint.
w: Don't apply pressure to a suspected skull fracture; a splint isn't used.
A bleeding wound is treated with direct pressure.
Internal bleeding needs EMS and treatment for shock.

alt.q: How long should Darian's splint be?
alt.a: Past the joints above and below
alt.ex: Splints should be long enough to immobilize the joint above and below the injury.
w: All the way down to the person's feet
As short as it can possibly be

alt.q: The passenger's arm looks deformed at the elbow. What should Darian avoid?
alt.ex: Do not realign a misshapen bone or joint; it may cause further injury.
w: Splinting it as it was found

sc.title: Darian at the car accident

items.q: One of the passengers in the vehicles is complaining of chest pain, which is known as which of the following?

alt.q: If the passenger has angina medication, what should Darian do?
alt.ex: If the person has medication for angina, assist them in taking it.

alt.q: What medication do many people with recurring chest pain carry?
alt.ex: Many people with recurring chest pain have nitroglycerin placed under the tongue.

sc.title: Darian at the car accident

This is part of the procedure.

This is part of the procedure.

alt.q: Which pressure point would Darian use for heavy bleeding from the arm?

w: That is for a leg wound.

sc.title: Darian at the car accident
sc.text: Darian is an emergency medical technician (EMT) in a rural area. One night while in the ambulance, Darian and the other EMTs on staff respond to a car accident. items.q: When approaching the people involved in the accident, Darian wears disposable gloves. What is this an example of?

alt.q: What item protects a rescuer when giving mouth-to-mouth breaths?

Only after EMS takes over the care
Only when the patient asks for it

items.q: Lack of oxygen to the heart muscle causes

alt.q: Damage to the heart muscle from a lack of oxygen is called what?
alt.ex: Heart muscle damage from lack of oxygen is a heart attack, or myocardial infarction.
w: That is a temporary brain event.

alt.q: Where can angina be felt in atypical cases, especially in females?
alt.ex: Angina can be felt in atypical places such as the jaw, back, or underarms.

items.q: The only time the injured should be moved is if their life is in danger by not moving them.

alt.q: If an injured person must be moved, the rescuer should try to keep the spine in straight alignment.

alt.ww: Don't move them unless life is at risk.

items.q: It is best not to remove the stinger from an insect bite.

alt.q: Tweezers are the best tool for removing a bee stinger.

items.q: Which of the following is the most realistic statement about acting to assist the injured in an emergency?

alt.q: How should a rescuer feel if their help does not lead to a good outcome?

w: Sure they should not help again

items.q: A child can drown in only a few inches of water.

items.q: Which of the following conditions is the result of the skin beginning to freeze?

w: That is freezing of the skin.

alt.q: Which event should make a rescuer suspect internal bleeding?

items.q: A tourniquet is rarely used in emergency care because it too often does more harm than good.
items.ex: A tourniquet is used only as a last resort to save a life because it can cause loss of the limb.
items.ww: It can cost the limb, so it is a last resort.

alt.q: A tourniquet should not be used on a snakebite.
alt.ex: For bites, do not apply a tourniquet; it may damage tissue and lead to amputation.
alt.ww: Don't use a tourniquet for bites.

alt.q: A tourniquet should be the first method tried to control any heavy bleeding.
alt.ex: Direct pressure comes first; a tourniquet is a last resort.

items.q: What is the most effective way to control external bleeding?
items.ex: Direct pressure with a clean cloth or sterile dressing is the main way to stop bleeding.
w: Elevation helps but works with direct pressure.
A pressure dressing frees the rescuer's hands but is secondary.
A tourniquet is a last resort.

alt.q: Why does direct pressure help stop bleeding?
alt.a: It lets the body's clotting work
alt.ex: Pressure slows blood flow so the body can use its natural clotting.
w: It pushes the blood back into the veins
It cools the wound down quickly
It kills germs in the wound

alt.q: When can a rescuer use a pressure dressing instead of holding pressure by hand?
alt.ex: A pressure dressing can be applied if the rescuer needs their hands free.

items.q: A spiral wrap is not effective for wrapping joints because the wrap tends to slip off easily.
items.ex: A spiral wrap tends to slip off joints, so a figure-eight wrap is used for joints.
items.ww: Spiral wraps slip off joints.

alt.q: A figure-eight wrap is used on joints such as the ankle because it secures both sides of the joint.
alt.ex: A figure-eight wrap secures both sides of a joint like the ankle, elbow, or wrist.

alt.q: A spiral wrap should be started at the end of the limb closest to the body.
alt.ex: Start a spiral wrap at the distal end to enhance circulation and decrease swelling.

items.q: What does the "R" mean in RICE, the mnemonic for treating bone, joint, and muscle injuries?
items.ex: In RICE, R stands for rest, meaning limit use of the injured part.
w: Remove clothing that restricts injured area

alt.q: In the RICE mnemonic, what does the 'I' stand for?
alt.ex: I is immobilize: stabilize the part with an elastic bandage or splint.
w: C is cold in this textbook.

alt.q: When should the 'E' (elevate) step of RICE be skipped?
alt.a: If raising it causes more pain
alt.ex: Don't elevate the injured part if raising it causes more pain.
w: If the injury is the arm, not the leg
If the cold pack is still on
If it happened in the morning

items.q: What should you look for if you are attempting to determine what happened and you suspect the ill or injured person may have a specific medical condition?
items.a: A Medic Alert necklace or bracelet
items.ex: A Medic Alert necklace or bracelet may show conditions such as diabetes, epilepsy, or heart problems.
w: A copy of the Good Samaritan Act
A copy of the law doesn't tell you the condition.
Bystanders help, but don't show the condition.
Implied consent is a legal concept, not an object.

alt.q: Besides necklaces and bracelets, how else might Medic Alert information be carried?
alt.a: On a card in a wallet
alt.ex: People may wear necklaces or bracelets or carry cards with the information.
w: On a sticker on the car
In a text to a friend

alt.q: Which condition might a Medic Alert bracelet show?
alt.ex: A Medic Alert may specify if the person is diabetic, epileptic, or has heart problems.

items.q: The goal of immediate treatment for poisonings is to get the poison out of the body by inducing vomiting.
items.ex: The goal is to get the poison out, but do not induce vomiting unless directed by medical personnel.
items.ww: Don't induce vomiting unless told to by medical staff.

alt.q: A substance that burned the throat when swallowed can burn it again if vomiting is induced.
alt.ex: Inducing vomiting for a substance that burned the GI tract will burn it on the way up too.

alt.q: Home remedies should be given right away for swallowed poisons before calling for help.
alt.ex: Do not give food, fluids, or home remedies unless directed by medical personnel.

items.q: Withdrawal from a drug to which an individual has become addicted can result in a life-threatening situation.
items.ex: If an addictive drug is stopped, the body may go through withdrawal that can be life-threatening.
items.ww: Withdrawal can be life-threatening.

alt.q: A person going through drug withdrawal may have seizures.
alt.ex: Withdrawal signs can include tremors, cold sweats, and seizures.

alt.q: A person in drug withdrawal does not need EMS since it is not dangerous.
alt.ex: Call EMS for withdrawal; it can create life-threatening situations.

items.q: First aid for a sprain includes applying heat to the injured area.
items.ex: Sprains are treated like strains: cold compresses, elevation, and rest, not heat.
items.ww: Use cold, not heat, on a sprain.

alt.q: A sprain is treated the same way as a muscle strain.
alt.ex: The textbook says first aid for a sprain is the same as for a muscle strain.

alt.q: Ice should be placed directly on the skin over a sprained ankle.
alt.ex: Don't place ice directly on the skin; wrap the cold pack in a thin, dry towel.

items.q: After applying a bandage or splint to a patient's extremity, you should always
items.a: Check the circulation to be sure there is adequate perfusion
items.ex: Always check circulation after applying splints, slings, and wraps to make sure there is adequate perfusion.
w: Consent is obtained before care, not after.

SAMPLE is used to gather information, not after bandaging.

alt.q: After a wrap, the person's fingers turn bluish. What should be done?
alt.ex: If there is no pulse or fingers turn bluish, loosen the dressing and rewrap it.
w: Raise the arm over the head
Leave it on until EMS arrives

alt.q: How is circulation checked after splinting a leg?
alt.a: Check for a pulse below the splint
